q: Which cranial nerve is completely decussated, innervating the contralateral superior oblique?
w: CN4 is the only fully crossed cranial nerve; it supplies the contralateral superior oblique.
k: CN4 = only fully decussated; contralateral SO.
decode: The fully DECUSSATED nerve to the CONTRALATERAL superior oblique is CN4 (trochlear). It is the only cranial nerve that exits dorsally and crosses completely.
ow: CN3 stays ipsilateral and runs most muscles, not the crossed SO.
CN5 is sensory to the face, not a crossed motor nerve.
CN6 runs the lateral rectus, uncrossed.
Correct. CN4 fully decussates to the contralateral superior oblique.

q: A pupil-involving CN3 palsy (ptosis, eye down-and-out, dilated fixed pupil) is concerning for:
w: Pupillomotor fibers run on the outside of CN3, so external compression (aneurysm) involves the pupil early. A surgical emergency.
k: Pupil-involving CN3 = compressive aneurysm until excluded.
decode: A PUPIL-INVOLVING CN3 palsy is a surgical red flag for a compressive aneurysm (pupil fibers ride on the outside, hit first by compression). Ischemic causes spare the pupil.
ow: Ischemia typically SPARES the pupil, so a blown pupil argues against it.
A blown-pupil CN3 palsy is never benign.
Myasthenia does not fix or dilate the pupil.
Correct. Pupil involvement means compression, classically an aneurysm.

q: In CN3 palsy, an ischemic (diabetic) cause classically:
w: Ischemia hits the inner motor fibers first and spares the outer pupillomotor fibers, so the pupil is spared.
k: Compressive = pupil blown; ischemic = pupil spared.
decode: An ISCHEMIC (diabetic) CN3 palsy classically SPARES the pupil, because the outer pupillary fibers keep their blood supply while the inner motor fibers infarct. Compression is what blows the pupil.
ow: A single CN3 palsy does not cause bilateral blindness.
Nystagmus is not a feature of a CN3 palsy.
Correct. Diabetic (ischemic) CN3 palsy spares the pupil.
Pupil dilation points to compression, not ischemia.

q: Corneal sensation is carried by which nerve?
w: The ophthalmic division (V1) of the trigeminal, via the nasociliary nerve, provides corneal sensation.
k: Corneal sensation = CN5 V1 (nasociliary).
decode: Corneal sensation is carried by CN5 (trigeminal, V1 ophthalmic branch). CN7 moves the lids, CN3 the muscles, CN2 is vision.
ow: CN7 is motor to the lids (blink), not corneal sensation.
Correct. CN5 (V1) carries corneal sensation.
CN3 is motor to eye muscles, not sensation.
CN2 is the optic nerve (vision), not sensation.

q: Which division of the trigeminal nerve is the smallest and purely sensory?
w: V1 (ophthalmic) is the smallest and purely sensory; V3 (mandibular) is the largest and mixed.
k: V1 = smallest, pure sensory; V3 = largest.
decode: The smallest, purely SENSORY trigeminal division is V1 (ophthalmic). V3 is the largest and carries motor fibers; V2 is sensory but larger.
ow: V3 is the largest and has a motor component.
Correct. V1 ophthalmic is the smallest, purely sensory division.
V2 is sensory but larger than V1.
The divisions differ; V3 has motor fibers, so not all are mixed.

q: Orbital cellulitis most commonly spreads from which sinus?
w: The thin lamina papyracea of the ethmoid shares the medial orbital wall, so ethmoiditis is the usual source.
k: Ethmoidal sinus → orbital cellulitis.
decode: Orbital cellulitis most often spreads from the ETHMOID sinus, across the paper-thin lamina papyracea on the medial wall. The other sinuses are less common routes.
ow: The sphenoid sits deeper; not the usual route.
The frontal sinus is a less common source.
The maxillary sinus is below the floor, less common.
Correct. The ethmoid sinus is the classic spread route.

q: Sphenoidal sinusitis is classically associated with which ocular complication?
w: The optic nerve runs above the sphenoid sinus, so sphenoiditis causes retrobulbar neuritis, not orbital cellulitis.
k: Sphenoidal sinus → retrobulbar neuritis (CN2).
decode: Sphenoid sinusitis sits next to the orbital apex and optic nerve, so its classic ocular complication is retrobulbar (optic) neuritis. Cellulitis is the ethmoid pattern.
ow: Orbital cellulitis is the ethmoid complication, not sphenoid.
Dacryocystitis is a tear-sac infection, unrelated.
A blowout fracture is traumatic, not infectious.
Correct. Sphenoid sinusitis classically causes retrobulbar neuritis.

q: Which cranial nerve mediates both eyelid closure and reflex lacrimal secretion?
w: CN7 closes the lids (orbicularis) and drives reflex tearing via the greater petrosal nerve.
k: CN7 = lid closure + reflex tearing.
decode: CN7 (facial) mediates both eyelid CLOSURE (orbicularis) and reflex LACRIMAL secretion (parasympathetic). CN5 is sensory; CN3 and CN6 move the globe.
ow: CN5 is sensory to the face and cornea, not lid closure.
CN3 elevates the lid and moves the eye, not closure.
Correct. CN7 closes the lids and drives reflex tearing.
CN6 runs the lateral rectus, not lid closure.

q: The optic nerve (CN2) and ophthalmic artery enter the orbit through the:
w: CN2 and the ophthalmic artery pass through the optic canal (lesser wing of sphenoid), not the SOF.
k: CN2 + ophthalmic artery = optic canal.
decode: The optic nerve (CN2) and ophthalmic artery enter through the OPTIC CANAL. The superior orbital fissure carries the eye-movement nerves instead.
ow: The superior orbital fissure carries CN3, 4, V1, 6, not the optic nerve.
The inferior orbital fissure carries V2 branches, not CN2.
Correct. CN2 and the ophthalmic artery use the optic canal.
Foramen rotundum transmits V2, not the optic nerve.

q: Which cranial nerve has the longest intracranial course?
w: CN4 has the longest intracranial course (~75 mm) and is also the thinnest motor nerve.
k: CN4 = longest intracranial course.
decode: CN4 (trochlear) has the longest intracranial course, looping around the brainstem before its dorsal exit. That long thin course makes it vulnerable to head trauma.
ow: CN3 has a shorter course than the trochlear.
Correct. CN4 has the longest intracranial course.
CN2 is a tract, and its course is shorter than CN4's.
CN6 has a long course but shorter than CN4's.

q: The lateral rectus is innervated by:
w: By the rule LR6 SO4 AO3: lateral rectus = CN6, superior oblique = CN4, all others = CN3.
k: LR6 SO4 AO3.
decode: The lateral rectus is run by CN6 (abducens), following the LR6 rule. CN4 is the superior oblique; CN3 runs the rest; CN5 is sensory.
ow: CN4 is the superior oblique, not the lateral rectus.
CN5 is sensory, not a motor nerve here.
Correct. LR6: the lateral rectus is CN6.
CN3 runs most other muscles, not the lateral rectus.

q: The primary visual cortex (area 17) is located in which lobe?
w: Area 17 (primary visual cortex) sits in the medial occipital lobe.
k: Area 17 = occipital lobe.
decode: The primary visual cortex (Brodmann area 17) sits in the OCCIPITAL lobe at the back of the brain. The other lobes are not primary vision.
ow: Correct. Area 17 is in the occipital lobe.
The temporal lobe handles hearing and memory.
The parietal lobe handles touch and spatial sense.
The frontal lobe handles planning and movement.

q: What is the PRIMARY action of the superior oblique muscle?
w: The SO's primary action is intorsion; depression is secondary (and abduction tertiary).
k: SO primary action = intorsion.
decode: The PRIMARY action of the superior oblique is INTORSION (its secondary actions are depression and abduction). Muscles running obliquely twist first.
ow: Abduction is a secondary, not primary, SO action.
Elevation is not a superior oblique action.
Depression is a secondary SO action, not primary.
Correct. The superior oblique's primary action is intorsion.

q: Which extraocular muscle does NOT originate from the annulus of Zinn?
w: The inferior oblique originates from the maxilla (orbital floor); all other EOMs arise from the annulus of Zinn.
k: IO = only EOM not from annulus of Zinn.
decode: The inferior oblique is the ONE extraocular muscle NOT arising from the annulus of Zinn; it originates near the orbital floor (maxilla). The four recti and superior oblique arise from the ring.
ow: The lateral rectus arises from the annulus of Zinn.
The superior rectus arises from the annulus.
The medial rectus arises from the annulus.
Correct. The inferior oblique arises from the orbital floor, not the ring.

q: The thinnest (weakest) orbital wall is the:
w: The medial wall (lamina papyracea of the ethmoid) is thinnest; the lateral wall is thickest.
k: Medial wall thinnest; lateral thickest.
decode: The thinnest, weakest orbital wall is the MEDIAL wall (lamina papyracea of the ethmoid), which is why infection and blowouts spread there. The floor is also thin but the medial wall is thinnest.
ow: The floor is thin (blowout site) but not the thinnest.
The roof is relatively thick.
Correct. The medial wall (lamina papyracea) is thinnest.
The lateral wall is the thickest, most protective.

q: The superior orbital fissure transmits all EXCEPT:
w: The SOF carries CN3, CN4, CN6, V1 branches, and the superior ophthalmic vein. CN2 goes through the optic canal.
k: CN2 = optic canal, not SOF.
decode: The superior orbital fissure transmits CN3, 4, V1, and 6, so the EXCEPTION is CN2 (which uses the optic canal). Pick the optic nerve.
ow: Correct. CN2 uses the optic canal, not the superior orbital fissure.
CN4 passes through the superior orbital fissure.
CN3 passes through the superior orbital fissure.
CN6 passes through the superior orbital fissure.

q: Which rectus muscle inserts NEAREST the limbus and is the strongest?
w: By the Spiral of Tillaux, the MR inserts nearest (5.5 mm) and is the strongest; SR inserts farthest (7.7 mm).
k: MR nearest (5.5 mm, strongest).
decode: The MEDIAL rectus inserts nearest the limbus (about 5.5 mm) and is the strongest rectus. The insertions follow the spiral of Tillaux, with medial closest.
ow: The lateral rectus inserts farther back than the medial.
The inferior rectus inserts farther than the medial.
The superior rectus inserts farthest of the horizontal/vertical recti.
Correct. The medial rectus inserts nearest the limbus and is strongest.

q: The longest extraocular muscle is the:
w: The superior oblique, including its tendon, is the longest EOM at ~60 mm.
k: SO = longest EOM (60 mm).
decode: The SUPERIOR OBLIQUE is the longest extraocular muscle (its long tendon loops through the trochlea). The recti and inferior oblique are shorter.
ow: The medial rectus is shorter than the superior oblique.
The inferior oblique is the shortest, not longest.
Correct. The superior oblique is the longest extraocular muscle.
The lateral rectus is shorter than the superior oblique.

q: A patient has vertical diplopia worse on downgaze and adduction, with a compensatory head tilt. The palsy is:
w: CN4/SO palsy gives vertical diplopia worst down-and-in, with a Bielschowsky head tilt to the opposite shoulder.
k: CN4 palsy = vertical diplopia + head tilt.
decode: Vertical diplopia worse on DOWNGAZE and ADDUCTION, with a compensatory head tilt, is a CN4 (superior oblique) palsy. The head tilt away is the Bielschowsky sign.
ow: CN7 is facial motor, not an eye-movement palsy.
CN3 palsy gives down-and-out eye and ptosis, not this pattern.
Correct. Downgaze/adduction diplopia with head tilt is a CN4 palsy.
CN6 palsy gives horizontal, not vertical, diplopia.

q: How do the rectus and oblique muscles insert relative to the equator?
o: Recti in front, obliques behind the equator
Both in front of the equator
w: The recti insert anterior to the equator; the obliques insert posterior to it.
k: Recti front of equator; obliques behind.
decode: The RECTI insert IN FRONT of the equator; the OBLIQUES insert BEHIND it. That front-recti, back-obliques arrangement lets the obliques tort and vertically act.
ow: Reversed; recti are in front, obliques behind.
Not both behind; recti are in front.
Correct. Recti insert in front, obliques behind the equator.
Not both in front; obliques insert behind.

q: Removal of the eye's internal contents while preserving the sclera and EOMs is called:
w: Evisceration removes only the internal contents (sclera stays). Enucleation removes the whole globe.
k: Evisceration = contents only; enucleation = whole globe.
decode: Removing the internal contents while KEEPING the sclera and muscles is evisceration. Enucleation removes the whole globe; exenteration removes the orbit's contents.
ow: Enucleation removes the whole globe, not just contents.
Correct. Evisceration keeps the scleral shell and muscles.
Exenteration removes the entire orbital contents.
Enucleation removes the globe, sclera included.

q: The suspensory ligament of the eyeball (a thickening of Tenon's capsule) is:
w: Lockwood's ligament (with IR and IO fascia) forms the suspensory hammock of the globe.
k: Lockwood's = suspensory ligament of the eye.
decode: The suspensory ligament of the eyeball, a thickening of Tenon's capsule that slings the globe, is Lockwood's ligament. Whitnall's slings the levator; the annulus is the muscle origin.
ow: Whitnall's ligament is the superior (levator) suspensory ligament.
Correct. Lockwood's ligament is the suspensory sling of the globe.
Check ligaments limit rectus muscle excursion, different structures.
The annulus of Zinn is the common muscle origin, not a sling.

q: How many bones form the bony orbit?
w: Seven bones: maxilla, frontal, sphenoid, zygomatic, lacrimal, palatine, ethmoid.
k: 7 orbital bones.
decode: Seven bones form the bony orbit: frontal, sphenoid, zygomatic, maxilla, ethmoid, lacrimal, and palatine. Not 5, 6, or 8.
ow: Fewer than the seven orbital bones.
Fewer than the seven orbital bones.
Correct. Seven bones form the orbit.
One more than the seven orbital bones.

q: The orbital septum is clinically important because it:
w: The septum separates preseptal (anterior, milder) from orbital (posterior, sight-threatening) infection.
k: Septum = preseptal vs orbital divide.
decode: The orbital SEPTUM matters because it SEPARATES the lid from the orbit, the barrier dividing preseptal from orbital cellulitis. It does not make tears, drain aqueous, or move the globe.
ow: Tears are made by lacrimal and meibomian glands, not the septum.
Correct. The septum separates the lid from the orbit.
Aqueous drains through the trabecular meshwork, not the septum.
The septum does not rotate the globe.

q: From outside in toward the cornea, the tear film layers are:
w: Outer lipid (anti-evaporative) → aqueous (bulk) → mucin (wets the cornea).
k: Lipid → aqueous → mucin.
decode: From outside (air) inward toward the cornea, the tear film is LIPID, then AQUEOUS, then MUCIN. Lipid outermost slows evaporation; mucin innermost anchors to the cornea.
ow: Correct. Lipid (outer), aqueous (middle), mucin (inner).
Mucin is innermost, not middle.
Reversed order; lipid is outermost, not innermost.
Lipid is the outer layer, not the middle.

q: Which is the thickest layer of the tear film?
w: Aqueous (~7 µm) is thickest; lipid (~0.5 µm) and mucin (~0.03 µm) are far thinner.
k: Aqueous is thickest (~7 µm).
decode: The AQUEOUS layer is by far the thickest tear layer (the bulk of tear volume). Lipid and mucin are thin films at the outer and inner surfaces.
ow: The layers are not equal; aqueous dominates.
The lipid layer is a thin outer film.
Correct. The aqueous layer is the thickest.
The mucin layer is a thin inner film.

q: The basic (resting) aqueous tear secretion comes from:
w: Krause and Wolfring provide basic aqueous; the main lacrimal gland is for reflex secretion (CN7).
k: Basic aqueous = Krause + Wolfring.
decode: BASIC (resting) aqueous tears come from the accessory glands of Krause and Wolfring. The MAIN lacrimal gland handles REFLEX tearing; goblet cells make mucin; meibomian glands make lipid.
ow: Correct. Krause and Wolfring make basal aqueous tears.
Goblet cells secrete mucin, not aqueous.
Meibomian glands secrete lipid, not aqueous.
The main gland provides reflex, not basal, secretion.

q: Schirmer's test measures, and TBUT measures, respectively:
w: Schirmer = aqueous volume (normal 10–25 mm/5 min); TBUT = stability (normal >10 s).
k: Schirmer = volume; TBUT = stability.
decode: Schirmer's measures aqueous VOLUME (strip wetting); TBUT measures tear film STABILITY (time to breakup). Match volume to Schirmer, stability to TBUT.
ow: Reversed; Schirmer is volume, TBUT is stability.
Schirmer measures volume, not stability.
Correct. Schirmer = aqueous volume; TBUT = film stability.
TBUT measures stability, not volume.

q: A patient has Schirmer's 18 mm but TBUT of 5 seconds. The likely problem is:
w: Normal aqueous volume with a short break-up time points to lipid-layer deficiency (MGD), i.e., evaporative dry eye.
k: Normal Schirmer + short TBUT = evaporative (MGD).
decode: Normal Schirmer (good volume) but short TBUT (unstable film) points to EVAPORATIVE dry eye (meibomian/lipid problem). Aqueous-deficient dry eye would give a LOW Schirmer.
ow: Punctal stenosis causes tearing overflow, not a short TBUT.
Aqueous deficiency would lower the Schirmer, which here is normal.
Correct. Normal Schirmer with short TBUT is evaporative dry eye.
Reflex hypersecretion raises tearing, not this pattern.

q: The nasolacrimal duct drains into the:
w: The NLD opens into the inferior meatus, guarded by the valve of Hasner.
k: NLD → inferior meatus (valve of Hasner).
decode: The nasolacrimal duct drains into the INFERIOR meatus (under the inferior turbinate). The other meatus drain paranasal sinuses.
ow: Correct. The nasolacrimal duct drains into the inferior meatus.
The superior meatus drains posterior ethmoid sinuses.
The middle meatus drains most anterior sinuses.
The sphenoethmoidal recess drains the sphenoid sinus.

q: Horner's syndrome produces what kind of ptosis?
w: Horner's paralyzes Müller's muscle, giving a mild 1–2 mm ptosis. Complete ptosis needs LPS (CN3) failure.
k: Müller's paralysis = 1–2 mm partial ptosis.
decode: Horner's paralyzes Müller's muscle (sympathetic), giving a PARTIAL ptosis (plus miosis, anhidrosis). Levator (CN3) palsy gives a complete ptosis; myasthenia gives fatiguable ptosis.
ow: A complete ptosis is a levator (CN3) problem, not Horner's.
Correct. Horner's gives partial ptosis from Müller's paralysis.
Horner's does produce a mild ptosis, not miosis alone.
Fatiguable ptosis is myasthenia, not Horner's.

q: The predominant immunoglobulin in tears is:
w: Secretory IgA is the major tear immunoglobulin, with lysozyme and lactoferrin for defense.
k: Tears = secretory IgA.
decode: The predominant tear immunoglobulin is IgA (secretory), the mucosal antibody. IgG, IgM, and IgE are minor in tears.
ow: IgM is not the predominant tear antibody.
IgG is present but not predominant in tears.
Correct. Secretory IgA predominates in tears.
IgE relates to allergy, not the main tear antibody.

q: 'Crocodile tears' (gustatory lacrimation) result from:
o: A tumor of the lacrimal gland
w: After a CN7 lesion, regenerating salivary fibers misroute to the lacrimal gland, so eating triggers tearing.
k: Crocodile tears = misdirected CN7 fibers.
decode: 'Crocodile tears' (tearing while eating) come from ABERRANT CN7 regeneration, misrouting salivary fibers to the lacrimal gland. It is not a tumor, dry eye, or punctal problem.
ow: Correct. Aberrant CN7 regeneration causes gustatory tearing.
A lacrimal gland tumor does not cause gustatory tearing.
Dry eye hypersecretion is reflex, not meal-triggered.
Punctal stenosis blocks drainage, not this.

q: Goblet cells, which secrete mucin, are absent at the:
w: Goblet cells are densest at the fornix and absent at the lid margins and limbus.
k: Goblet cells absent at lid margins + limbus.
decode: Goblet cells (mucin) populate the conjunctiva but are ABSENT at the lid margins and limbus (transition zones). They are densest in the fornix and plica.
ow: The fornix is rich in goblet cells.
The bulbar conjunctiva contains goblet cells.
The plica semilunaris is goblet-cell rich.
Correct. Goblet cells are absent at the lid margins and limbus.

q: A 6-week-old with unilateral epiphora and mucopurulent discharge since birth most likely has:
w: A non-canalized NLD (failure at the valve of Hasner) causes stasis, infection, and chronic discharge.
k: Infant epiphora + discharge = NLD obstruction/dacryocystitis.
decode: A newborn with epiphora and mucopurulent discharge since birth has congenital nasolacrimal duct OBSTRUCTION (a blocked, infected sac). Gonococcal conjunctivitis appears in the first days; congenital glaucoma gives a cloudy enlarged cornea.
ow: Gland agenesis causes dryness, not watering and discharge.
Gonococcal conjunctivitis is hyperacute in the first days of life.
Correct. Congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction fits epiphora since birth.
Congenital glaucoma gives a cloudy, enlarged cornea, not discharge.

q: The cornea contributes about how much refractive power, making it the strongest lens of the eye?
w: The cornea provides ~43 D, the most of any ocular refracting surface.
k: Cornea ~43 D (strongest refractor).
decode: The cornea provides about 43 D, the eye's STRONGEST refracting surface (air-to-tissue interface). The lens adds about 19 D. Pick the larger corneal value.
ow: 10 D is far too low for the cornea.
19 D is roughly the LENS power, not the cornea.
Correct. The cornea contributes about 43 D.
59 D is the whole eye's power, not the cornea alone.

q: Which corneal layer makes up about 90% of corneal thickness?
w: The stroma is ~90% of corneal thickness; the epithelium is ~10% of weight.
k: Stroma = 90% of thickness.
decode: The STROMA is about 90% of corneal thickness (regularly packed collagen). Epithelium, Bowman's, and endothelium are thin layers.
ow: Bowman's is a thin acellular layer.
Correct. The stroma is about 90% of corneal thickness.
The endothelium is a single cell layer.
The epithelium is only a few cell layers.

q: Which corneal layer CANNOT regenerate after injury?
w: Bowman's (and the endothelium) cannot regenerate; epithelium and Descemet's can.
k: Bowman's + endothelium do not regenerate.
decode: BOWMAN'S membrane cannot regenerate; injury to it heals with scar. The epithelium regenerates readily; Descemet's can be re-secreted by endothelium.
ow: The epithelium regenerates quickly.
Correct. Bowman's membrane does not regenerate and scars.
Descemet's can be re-formed by the endothelium.
The tear film is not a corneal layer that regenerates.

q: Corneal thickness is:
w: The cornea is thinner centrally (~0.52–0.56 mm) and thickens toward the periphery (0.7–1.0 mm).
k: Cornea thinner centrally.
decode: The cornea is THINNER CENTRALLY (~0.52 mm) and thicker peripherally (~0.65 mm). It is not uniform, and it is not thickest centrally.
ow: It is actually thicker, not thinnest, at the limbus.
It is not uniform; center is thinner.
Reversed; the center is thinner, not thicker.
Correct. The cornea is thinner centrally than peripherally.

q: Corneal deturgescence (clarity) is maintained by:
w: The endothelial Na-K ATPase pumps ions and draws water out of the stroma, keeping it clear.
k: Endothelial Na-K ATPase = deturgescence.
decode: Corneal clarity (deturgescence, staying dehydrated) is maintained by the ENDOTHELIAL Na-K pump that draws water out. Bowman's, tears, and mucin do not run the pump.
ow: Evaporation is minor; the pump keeps the cornea clear.
Bowman's provides structure, not fluid control.
Mucin anchors the tear film, not corneal hydration.
Correct. The endothelial Na-K pump keeps the cornea deturgescent.

q: Fuchs' endothelial dystrophy causes corneal edema because:
o: Endothelial cell loss disables the pump
w: Endothelium is post-mitotic; once cell density falls too low, the pump fails and the stroma swells.
k: Fuchs' = endothelial loss → pump failure → edema.
decode: Fuchs' dystrophy loses ENDOTHELIAL cells, disabling the pump, so fluid builds up and the cornea swells. It is not a Bowman's, goblet, or epithelial problem.
ow: Bowman's is not the failing layer in Fuchs'.
Correct. Endothelial loss disables the pump, causing edema.
Goblet cells make mucin, unrelated to corneal edema.
Epithelial junctions are not the Fuchs' defect.

q: The sclera is thickest at which point?
w: The sclera is thickest (~1.0 mm) at the CN2 entrance and thinnest (~0.3 mm) under the EOM insertions.
k: Sclera thickest at CN2; thinnest at EOM insertion.
decode: The sclera is THICKEST at the OPTIC NERVE entrance (~1 mm) and thinnest under the rectus insertions. The nerve entrance anchors the tough coat.
ow: Under the rectus insertions the sclera is thinnest.
The limbus is a transition, not the thickest point.
The equator is intermediate, not the thickest.
Correct. The sclera is thickest at the optic nerve entrance.

q: Why is the cornea transparent but the sclera white?
o: The sclera is much thicker than cornea
The cornea is more vascular than sclera
w: Uniform corneal collagen spacing transmits light; the sclera's irregular, interlacing fibers scatter it (opaque).
k: Regular collagen = clear; irregular = white.
decode: The cornea is clear because its collagen is REGULARLY, uniformly spaced (destructive interference of scatter); scleral collagen is irregular, so it scatters all light and looks white.
ow: Both are mostly collagen; spacing, not cell type, is the key.
Thickness is not why the sclera is opaque.
Correct. Regular corneal collagen spacing gives transparency.
The cornea is avascular, not more vascular, than sclera.

q: The cornea is innervated by the nasociliary nerve in all layers EXCEPT:
w: Sensory innervation reaches all layers except Descemet's and the endothelium.
k: All corneal layers innervated except Descemet's/endothelium.
decode: The nasociliary (CN5) nerves supply the cornea except DESCEMET'S and the ENDOTHELIUM (the deep non-innervated layers). The anterior layers are richly innervated.
ow: Correct. Descemet's and endothelium lack corneal innervation.
The stroma and Bowman's ARE innervated.
The epithelium and stroma are innervated.
The epithelium and Bowman's are innervated.

q: A descemetocele is:
o: An ectasia of the anterior sclera
A defect of the corneal epithelium
w: In a descemetocele, the stroma has perforated but the elastic Descemet's membrane remains intact and bulges forward.
k: Descemetocele = intact Descemet's bulging through stroma.
decode: A descemetocele is Descemet's membrane BULGING through a thinned stroma (deep ulcer down to Descemet's), a pre-perforation emergency. It is not a scleral ectasia, a simple tear, or an epithelial defect.
ow: An anterior scleral ectasia is a staphyloma, not a descemetocele.
A rupture is a break; a descemetocele is an intact bulge.
Correct. A descemetocele is Descemet's bulging through the stroma.
An epithelial defect is superficial, not down to Descemet's.

q: On gonioscopy, the most anterior landmark, a glistening line at the end of Descemet's, is:
w: Schwalbe's line marks the termination of Descemet's membrane, the most anterior angle landmark.
k: Schwalbe's line = most anterior angle landmark.
decode: The most anterior gonioscopy landmark, a glistening line at the end of Descemet's, is Schwalbe's line. Moving posteriorly you then reach the trabecular meshwork, scleral spur, and ciliary body band.
ow: The trabecular meshwork lies just behind Schwalbe's line.
The ciliary body band is the most posterior landmark.
Correct. Schwalbe's line is the most anterior angle landmark.
The scleral spur lies posterior to the meshwork.

q: The horizontal corneal diameter relative to the vertical is:
w: The cornea is oval, wider horizontally (~11–12 mm) than vertically (~10–11 mm).
k: Cornea oval, wider horizontally.
decode: The horizontal corneal diameter (~12 mm) is LARGER than the vertical (~11 mm), so the cornea is a slightly wider oval. Not equal or smaller.
ow: It is a fixed shape, not gaze-dependent.
The two diameters are not equal.
Correct. The horizontal corneal diameter is larger than the vertical.
The horizontal is larger, not smaller.

q: The uveal tract consists of:
w: The uvea is the vascular middle coat: iris, ciliary body, and choroid.
k: Uvea = iris + ciliary body + choroid.
decode: The uveal tract is the middle vascular coat: IRIS, CILIARY BODY, and CHOROID. The lens, vitreous, sclera, cornea, and retina are not uvea.
ow: Correct. The uvea is iris, ciliary body, and choroid.
The lens and vitreous are not uveal structures.
The sclera and retina are separate coats.
The cornea, lens, and retina are not the uvea.

q: During accommodation, the ciliary muscle contracts and:
o: Has no effect on the lens
Tightens the zonules, flattening the lens
Relaxes the zonules, letting the lens round up
w: Ciliary contraction reduces the ring diameter, slackening zonules so the elastic lens rounds up (more power).
k: Ciliary contracts → zonules relax → lens rounds.
decode: In accommodation the ciliary muscle CONTRACTS, which RELAXES the zonules, letting the elastic lens ROUND UP (more power) for near focus. The tightening/flattening option is the resting, distance state.
ow: The ciliary muscle strongly affects lens shape.
Tightening zonules and flattening is the resting (distance) state.
The lens rounds up, it does not move backward.
Correct. Ciliary contraction relaxes zonules so the lens rounds up.

q: The preferred surgical entry into the eye for vitreoretinal procedures is the:
w: The pars plana is the least vascular ciliary body zone, minimizing bleeding on entry.
k: Pars plana = safe surgical entry.
decode: Vitreoretinal surgery enters through the PARS PLANA, a safe zone with no retina or major vessels, about 3-4 mm behind the limbus. The pars plicata, iris root, and limbus are unsafe entries.
ow: The pars plicata has ciliary processes; not the safe entry.
The iris root is anterior and vascular, not the entry.
Correct. The pars plana is the safe surgical entry.
The limbus is the anterior-segment entry, not for vitreoretinal work.

q: The sphincter pupillae is innervated by:
w: The sphincter (miosis) is parasympathetic (CN3 via the ciliary ganglion); the dilator is sympathetic.
k: Sphincter = parasympathetic CN3.
decode: The sphincter pupillae (constrictor) is run by PARASYMPATHETIC CN3 fibers. The dilator is sympathetic; CN5 is sensory, CN7 motor to the face.
ow: Correct. Parasympathetic CN3 drives the sphincter (miosis).
CN7 is facial motor, not iris sphincter.
CN5 is sensory, not the sphincter's nerve.
Sympathetic fibers run the DILATOR, not the sphincter.

q: The choroid is thickest at the:
w: The choroid is thickest at the posterior pole and thinnest anteriorly.
k: Choroid thickest at posterior pole.
decode: The choroid is thickest at the POSTERIOR POLE (highest metabolic demand near the macula) and thins toward the ora serrata. Pick the back of the eye.
ow: The choroid is thinnest near the ora serrata.
The equator is intermediate thickness.
The anterior periphery is thin choroid.
Correct. The choroid is thickest at the posterior pole.

q: Bilateral small, irregular pupils that constrict to near but not to light indicate:
w: Light-near dissociation with small irregular pupils is Argyll-Robertson (neurosyphilis, pretectal lesion).
k: Argyll-Robertson = light-near dissociation, neurosyphilis.
decode: Bilateral small, irregular pupils with light-near dissociation (react to near, not light) are Argyll-Robertson pupils (neurosyphilis). Adie's is a large tonic pupil; Horner's is small but reacts to light.
ow: A Marcus-Gunn pupil is an afferent defect, not this.
Correct. Light-near dissociation with small irregular pupils is Argyll-Robertson.
Horner's is a small pupil that still reacts to light.
Adie's is a large tonic pupil, not small and bilateral.

q: An Adie's tonic pupil is caused by a lesion at the:
w: Adie's results from ciliary ganglion damage; it constricts to dilute (0.125%) pilocarpine from denervation supersensitivity.
k: Adie's = ciliary ganglion (benign).
decode: An Adie's tonic pupil comes from a lesion at the CILIARY GANGLION / short ciliary nerves (postganglionic parasympathetic). This denervation gives supersensitivity to dilute pilocarpine.
ow: The chiasm handles vision fibers, not the tonic pupil.
Correct. Adie's is a ciliary ganglion / short ciliary nerve lesion.
The pretectal nucleus is the light-reflex relay, not Adie's site.
The superior cervical ganglion is sympathetic (Horner's), not Adie's.

q: Dilute 0.125% pilocarpine constricts which pupil?
w: Normal pupils do not respond to this low dose; an Adie's pupil constricts due to supersensitivity.
k: 0.125% pilocarpine constricts Adie's (not normal).
decode: Dilute 0.125% pilocarpine constricts a tonic ADIE'S pupil (denervation supersensitivity) but not a normal pupil. That weak-dose constriction is the diagnostic tell.
ow: Argyll-Robertson pupils are not defined by this supersensitivity test.
A normal pupil does not react to such a weak dose.
Horner's is diagnosed with cocaine/apraclonidine, not this.
Correct. A tonic Adie's pupil constricts to dilute pilocarpine.

q: The dilator pupillae lies in which zone of the iris?
w: The radial dilator occupies the peripheral (ciliary) zone; the circular sphincter sits in the central pupillary zone.
k: Dilator = ciliary zone; sphincter = pupillary zone.
decode: The dilator pupillae lies in the CILIARY zone (outer iris), radiating like spokes; the sphincter sits in the pupillary zone (inner ring). Match dilator to the outer ciliary zone.
ow: The dilator spans the ciliary zone, not just the root.
Correct. The dilator pupillae lies in the ciliary zone.
The pupillary zone holds the sphincter, not the dilator.
The posterior pigment epithelium is separate from the dilator muscle.

q: The choriocapillaris supplies which part of the retina?
w: The choriocapillaris feeds the outer retina (65–85% of retinal blood flow); the central retinal artery feeds the inner layers.
k: Choriocapillaris = outer retina.
decode: The choriocapillaris (from the choroid) supplies the OUTER retina (photoreceptors, RPE) by diffusion; the central retinal artery supplies the INNER retina. Match choroid to outer.
ow: Correct. The choriocapillaris supplies the outer retina.
The inner retina is fed by the central retinal artery.
The two supplies split the retina, not equally shared.
It supplies the outer retina broadly, not only the fovea.

q: The layer between the choroid and the RPE is:
w: Bruch's membrane (~7 µm) separates the choriocapillaris from the RPE; it is involved in ARMD (drusen).
k: Bruch's membrane sits between choroid and RPE.
decode: Between the choroid and the RPE lies BRUCH'S membrane (the basement complex where drusen deposit). The lamina cribrosa is at the optic nerve; the ILM is the innermost retina.
ow: Correct. Bruch's membrane lies between choroid and RPE.
The lamina cribrosa is at the optic nerve head.
The sclera is the outer coat, external to the choroid.
The internal limiting membrane is the innermost retinal layer.

q: The normal resting pupil diameter is about:
w: Normal pupil size is ~3–4 mm; <1.5 mm is miotic and >5 mm is mydriatic.
k: Normal pupil 3–4 mm.
decode: The normal resting pupil is about 3-4 mm in room light. 1 mm is a pinpoint; 6-8 mm is a dilated pupil.
ow: 1 mm is a pinpoint (miotic) pupil.
6 mm is a dilated pupil, not resting.
8 mm is markedly dilated.
Correct. The resting pupil is about 3-4 mm.

q: Aqueous humor is produced by the:
w: The non-pigmented ciliary epithelium of the pars plicata secretes aqueous at ~2 µL/min.
k: Aqueous from non-pigment ciliary epithelium.
decode: Aqueous is produced by the NON-PIGMENTED ciliary epithelium (of the ciliary processes). The trabecular meshwork is the DRAIN, not the source; the lens epithelium and choriocapillaris are unrelated.
ow: The lens epithelium does not make aqueous.
The choriocapillaris supplies the outer retina, not aqueous.
The trabecular meshwork drains aqueous, it does not make it.
Correct. The non-pigmented ciliary epithelium produces aqueous.

q: What percentage of aqueous outflow is via the trabecular meshwork?
w: ~80% drains through the trabecular (conventional) route; ~20% via uveoscleral. Prostaglandins boost uveoscleral.
k: Trabecular 80%, uveoscleral 20%.
decode: About 80% of aqueous leaves through the TRABECULAR (conventional) meshwork; the remaining ~20% goes uveoscleral. Match the meshwork to the larger share.
ow: 20% is the UVEOSCLERAL share, not trabecular.
50% understates the trabecular route.
Correct. About 80% of outflow is trabecular.
Not 100%; some outflow is uveoscleral.

q: Which lens capsule region is thickest (and the thickest basement membrane in the body)?
w: The anterior capsule (~15 µm) is the thickest BM in the body; the posterior (~2.2 µm) is thinnest.
k: Anterior capsule thickest; posterior thinnest.
decode: The ANTERIOR lens capsule is the thickest region and the thickest basement membrane in the body (it keeps thickening with age). The posterior capsule is thinnest.
ow: Correct. The anterior capsule is the thickest basement membrane in the body.
The regions differ; anterior is thickest.
The posterior capsule is the thinnest region.
The equatorial capsule is not the thickest.

q: The primary mechanism of presbyopia is:
w: Lifelong fiber compaction hardens the nucleus so it cannot round up even when zonular tension is released.
k: Presbyopia = lens nuclear hardening.
decode: Presbyopia is primarily the HARDENING (sclerosis) of the lens nucleus, so it can no longer round up. It is not zonule rupture, lens displacement, or ciliary atrophy.
ow: Zonules do not rupture in presbyopia.
The lens does not displace in presbyopia.
The ciliary muscle is relatively preserved; the lens stiffens.
Correct. Presbyopia is mainly lens nucleus hardening.

q: The vitreous gel is approximately:
w: Vitreous is ~98.5% water; hyaluronic acid gives it its gel character. Volume ~4.5 mL.
k: Vitreous ~98.5% water (hyaluronic acid).
decode: The vitreous is about 98-99% water (with collagen and hyaluronan giving the gel). It is not pure water or as low as 75%.
ow: Not quite 100%; it has collagen and hyaluronan.
Far too low; vitreous is mostly water.
Correct. The vitreous is about 98.5% water.
Higher than 75%; vitreous is about 98-99% water.

q: Compared with plasma, aqueous humor has:
w: Aqueous is protein-poor but has a much higher ascorbate concentration than plasma (antioxidant role).
k: Aqueous = high ascorbate, low protein.
decode: Aqueous has MORE ASCORBIC ACID (vitamin C) than plasma, an antioxidant concentrated in the eye. It has LESS protein and glucose than plasma and similar osmolarity.
ow: Aqueous has far LESS protein than plasma.
Aqueous osmolarity is similar to plasma, not clearly lower.
Aqueous glucose is lower than plasma.
Correct. Aqueous has more ascorbic acid than plasma.

q: Normal intraocular pressure ranges from:
w: Normal IOP is 10–21 mmHg; episcleral venous pressure (~10 mmHg) sets the floor.
k: Normal IOP 10–21 mmHg.
decode: Normal IOP is 10-21 mmHg. Higher ranges are elevated; 5-10 is low (hypotony).
ow: Correct. Normal IOP is 10-21 mmHg.
30-40 is markedly elevated.
22-30 is elevated (ocular hypertension range).
5-10 is low, toward hypotony.

q: How does aqueous humor differ from vitreous?
o: Vitreous is made by the ciliary body
Aqueous is replaced; vitreous is not
w: Aqueous is continuously produced and drained; vitreous gel is developmental and not replaced if lost.
k: Aqueous flows; vitreous gel is not replaced.
decode: Aqueous is continuously produced and REPLACED (turnover); vitreous is formed once and NOT replaced. That turnover difference is the key contrast.
ow: Aqueous fills the anterior segment; vitreous fills the posterior.
Vitreous is embryologic, not made by the ciliary body.
They differ in composition and turnover.
Correct. Aqueous turns over; vitreous does not.

q: The remnant of the embryonic hyaloid artery passing through the vitreous is:
w: Cloquet's canal is the hyaloid remnant, ending at the area of Martegiani near the disc.
k: Cloquet's canal = hyaloid remnant.
decode: The hyaloid artery remnant running through the vitreous is Cloquet's canal (from lens to disc). The ora serrata, Bruch's, and lamina cribrosa are unrelated structures.
ow: The ora serrata is the retina's anterior edge.
Correct. Cloquet's canal is the hyaloid artery remnant.
Bruch's membrane lies between choroid and RPE.
The lamina cribrosa is at the optic nerve head.

q: Which class of glaucoma drug lowers IOP mainly by increasing uveoscleral outflow?
w: Prostaglandins increase the uveoscleral (~20%) outflow pathway; the others mostly cut production.
k: Prostaglandins boost uveoscleral outflow.
decode: PROSTAGLANDIN analogs lower IOP mainly by increasing UVEOSCLERAL outflow. The others reduce aqueous PRODUCTION (CAI, beta blockers, alpha-2) or add some trabecular outflow.
ow: Correct. Prostaglandin analogs increase uveoscleral outflow.
Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors cut aqueous production.
Alpha-2 agonists mainly reduce production.
Beta blockers reduce aqueous production.

q: The posterior lens surface, compared to the anterior, is:
w: The posterior surface (radius ~6 mm) is more curved than the anterior (~10 mm), giving it more power.
k: Posterior lens surface more curved (steeper).
decode: The POSTERIOR lens surface is MORE curved (steeper) than the anterior. Both are convex, but the back is steeper.
ow: The lens is avascular, but the question is about curvature.
The two surfaces are not identical; the back is steeper.
Correct. The posterior lens surface is more curved.
The posterior surface is more, not less, curved.

q: Why is the crystalline lens avascular?
o: It is too small for vessels
Vessels would obstruct the optical path
w: Any vasculature would scatter light and blur the image, so the lens relies on aqueous for nutrition.
k: Lens avascular to stay optically clear.
decode: The lens is AVASCULAR because blood vessels would scatter light and obstruct the OPTICAL PATH; it lives on aqueous nutrition instead. It is not about size or lack of metabolism.
ow: Size is not why it lacks vessels.
Correct. Vessels would block the optical path, so it stays avascular.
The lens is not replaced daily; fibers are retained for life.
The lens does have metabolic needs, met by the aqueous.

q: A retinal detachment separates which two layers?
w: Detachment occurs at the potential space between the neurosensory photoreceptors and the RPE.
k: RD plane = photoreceptors vs RPE.
decode: A (rhegmatogenous) retinal detachment separates the neurosensory retina (PHOTORECEPTORS) from the RPE, along the old embryonic cleft. It is not an RPE-Bruch's or choroid-sclera split.
ow: Correct. Detachment separates photoreceptors from the RPE.
RPE-Bruch's separation is a PED, not a retinal detachment.
NFL-ganglion is within the neural retina, not the detachment plane.
Choroid-sclera separation is a choroidal detachment.

q: The foveola contains:
o: Equal numbers of rods and cones
w: The foveola is pure cones, rod-free and capillary-free, giving peak acuity.
k: Foveola = pure cones, capillary-free.
decode: The foveola contains CONES ONLY and is AVASCULAR (no capillaries), giving the sharpest vision. No rods and no vessels is the tell.
ow: The foveola is cone-only, not a rod-cone mix.
Correct. The foveola is cones only, with no capillaries.
The foveola has cones, not rods.
It is packed with cones, not devoid of photoreceptors.

q: Which retinal region is THICKEST?
w: The parafovea is thickest (piled-up displaced ganglion cells); the foveola is the thinnest retina.
k: Parafovea thickest; foveola thinnest.
decode: The retina is THICKEST at the PARAFOVEA (piled-up ganglion cells around the fovea). The foveola is thinnest; the ora serrata and disc are edges.
ow: The ora serrata is thin peripheral retina.
Correct. The parafovea is the thickest retina.
The foveola is the thinnest point, not thickest.
The optic disc is nerve fibers exiting, not thickest retina.

q: The physiologic blind spot corresponds to the:
w: The optic disc has no photoreceptors, producing the physiologic blind spot.
k: Optic disc = blind spot (no photoreceptors).
decode: The physiologic blind spot corresponds to the OPTIC DISC, which has no photoreceptors. Not the macula, fovea, or ora serrata.
ow: The macula is the sharpest-vision area, not the blind spot.
The ora serrata is the peripheral retinal edge.
The fovea is the point of sharpest vision.
Correct. The blind spot is the optic disc (no photoreceptors).

q: A normal cup-to-disc ratio is:
w: Normal C/D is ≤0.3; 0.5 is suspicious and 0.8 is highly concerning for glaucoma.
k: Normal C/D ≤0.3.
decode: A normal cup-to-disc ratio is 0.3 or less. Larger ratios (0.5-0.8) suggest glaucomatous cupping.
ow: Correct. A normal cup-to-disc ratio is about 0.3 or less.
0.8 is markedly cupped, suspicious for glaucoma.
0.7 is enlarged cupping, not normal.
0.5 is borderline/enlarged, not clearly normal.

q: Retinal diseases typically present with painless vision loss because:
o: The retina has no pain fibers
w: The retina lacks pain innervation, so disease is painless and often detected late.
k: Retina has no pain fibers.
decode: Retinal disease is PAINLESS because the retina has NO pain (sensory) fibers. Not because the cornea masks pain or it heals fast.
ow: The cornea does not mask retinal pain.
Retinal loss can be sudden, so 'always gradual' is wrong.
Correct. The retina has no pain fibers, so disease is painless.
The retina does not heal quickly; that is not why it is painless.

q: The inner retinal layers are supplied by:
w: The central retinal artery supplies the inner retina; the choriocapillaris supplies the outer retina.
k: Inner retina = central retinal artery.
decode: The INNER retina is supplied by the CENTRAL RETINAL ARTERY; the outer retina relies on the choriocapillaris. Match inner to the central retinal artery.
ow: Bruch's is a membrane, not a blood supply.
Correct. The central retinal artery supplies the inner retina.
The choriocapillaris supplies the OUTER retina.
The ciliary arteries supply the uvea, not the inner retina.

q: The macular pigments that filter blue light (and are targeted by AREDS2) are:
w: Lutein and zeaxanthin (xanthophylls) concentrate in the macula and are protective antioxidants.
k: Macular pigment = lutein + zeaxanthin.
decode: The macular pigments that filter blue light (and are in AREDS2) are LUTEIN and ZEAXANTHIN (carotenoids). Not hemoglobin, melanin, or the visual pigments.
ow: Correct. Lutein and zeaxanthin are the macular carotenoids.
Hemoglobin carries oxygen, not a macular filter.
Melanin and lipofuscin are RPE pigments, not the AREDS2 carotenoids.
Rhodopsin and iodopsin are visual (photoreceptor) pigments.

q: The ora serrata, the anterior termination of the retina, lies about:
w: The ora serrata is ~6 mm from the limbus, the junction of retina and pars plana.
k: Ora serrata ~6 mm from limbus.
decode: The ora serrata (anterior retinal edge) lies about 6 mm behind the limbus. The pars plana entry sits just anterior to it. 12 mm and 1 mm are wrong distances.
ow: The ora serrata is anterior to the equator.
12 mm is too far back.
Correct. The ora serrata is about 6 mm from the limbus.
1 mm is far too close to the limbus.

q: In glaucoma, which cells are primarily damaged at the lamina cribrosa?
w: Elevated IOP compresses retinal ganglion cell axons at the lamina cribrosa, causing field loss and cupping.
k: Glaucoma damages RGC axons at the lamina cribrosa.
decode: Glaucoma primarily damages RETINAL GANGLION CELL AXONS as they pass through the lamina cribrosa. Photoreceptors, bipolar cells, and RPE are not the primary target.
ow: Photoreceptors are not the glaucoma target.
Bipolar and amacrine cells are not primarily damaged.
Correct. Ganglion cell axons are damaged at the lamina cribrosa.
The RPE is not the glaucoma target.

q: The optic disc is located approximately:
o: Just anterior to the ora serrata
w: The disc sits ~3 mm nasal to the macula and ~0.8 mm above the foveola.
k: Disc ~3 mm nasal to macula.
decode: The optic disc sits about 3 mm NASAL to the foveola (and slightly superior). That nasal position is why the blind spot is temporal in the field.
ow: The disc is not at the fovea; that is the sharpest-vision spot.
The disc is nasal, not temporal, to the macula.
The disc is at the posterior pole, not near the ora serrata.
Correct. The disc lies about 3 mm nasal to the foveola.

q: How many layers does the retina have, counting from RPE to the inner limiting membrane?
w: Eleven layers: RPE, photoreceptors, ELM, ONL, Henle, OPL, INL, IPL, GCL, NFL, ILM.
k: Retina = 11 layers.
decode: The retina is classically described as 10 neural layers plus the RPE, giving 11 layers from RPE to the inner limiting membrane. Not 7, 9, or 13.
ow: Too few; the retina has 11 layers counting the RPE.
Too few; the classic count is 11.
Correct. Eleven layers from the RPE to the ILM.
Too many; the classic count is 11.

q: A complete optic nerve lesion causes:
w: Before the chiasm, an optic nerve lesion blinds the entire same-side eye.
k: Optic nerve lesion = ipsilateral blindness.
decode: A complete OPTIC NERVE lesion blinds that ONE eye entirely (ipsilateral total blindness), because it is before the chiasm. Hemianopias require chiasmal or retrochiasmal lesions.
ow: A contralateral hemianopia needs a tract/radiation lesion.
Correct. A complete optic nerve lesion causes ipsilateral total blindness.
Bitemporal loss is a chiasm lesion, not one nerve.
Quadrantanopia is a radiation lesion, not the optic nerve.

q: Which fibers cross at the optic chiasm?
w: Nasal retinal fibers decussate; temporal fibers stay ipsilateral. Chiasm damage gives bitemporal loss.
k: Nasal fibers cross at the chiasm.
decode: At the chiasm the NASAL retinal fibers CROSS (carrying the temporal fields); temporal fibers stay uncrossed. That is why chiasm lesions give bitemporal loss.
ow: Some fibers do cross at the chiasm.
Correct. Nasal retinal fibers cross at the chiasm.
Temporal fibers stay uncrossed; nasal fibers cross.
Only the nasal fibers cross, not all.

q: Bitemporal hemianopia is most commonly caused by:
w: A pituitary adenoma pushes up on the chiasm, damaging crossing nasal fibers and losing both temporal fields.
k: Bitemporal hemianopia = chiasm (pituitary).
decode: Bitemporal hemianopia comes from CHIASM compression, classically a PITUITARY adenoma pressing the crossing nasal fibers from below. Retina, occipital, and optic nerve lesions give other patterns.
ow: A retinal detachment gives a localized monocular defect.
An occipital stroke gives homonymous, not bitemporal, loss.
Retrobulbar neuritis blinds one eye, not both temporal fields.
Correct. A pituitary adenoma compresses the chiasm, causing bitemporal hemianopia.

q: An optic tract lesion produces:
w: Tract lesions give incongruous homonymous hemianopia; Wernicke's hemianopic pupil can occur here.
k: Optic tract = incongruous HH + Wernicke's pupil.
decode: An OPTIC TRACT lesion gives an INCONGRUOUS homonymous hemianopia (the two eyes' defects differ), because fibers are not yet neatly aligned. Congruity increases more posteriorly.
ow: A central scotoma is a macular/optic nerve pattern.
Bitemporal loss is a chiasm lesion.
Congruous defects come from posterior (occipital) lesions.
Correct. Optic tract lesions give incongruous homonymous hemianopia.

q: A temporal lobe (Meyer's loop) lesion causes:
w: Inferior retinal fibers loop through the temporal lobe; damage gives a contralateral superior quadrant defect.
k: Meyer's loop = 'pie in the sky' (superior).
decode: A TEMPORAL lobe (Meyer's loop) lesion knocks out the CONTRALATERAL SUPERIOR quadrant ('pie in the sky'). Meyer's loop carries upper-field (inferior retinal) fibers.
ow: Inferior quadrantanopia is a parietal lesion, not temporal.
Correct. Meyer's loop lesion gives a contralateral superior quadrantanopia.
Bitemporal loss is a chiasm lesion.
Tunnel vision is not a temporal-lobe pattern.

q: A parietal radiation lesion causes:
w: Superior retinal fibers run through the parietal lobe; damage produces an inferior quadrantanopia.
k: Parietal lesion = inferior quadrantanopia.
decode: A PARIETAL radiation lesion gives a CONTRALATERAL INFERIOR quadrantanopia ('pie on the floor'). Parietal fibers carry lower-field (superior retinal) information.
ow: Superior quadrantanopia is a temporal (Meyer's loop) lesion.
A central scotoma is not a radiation pattern.
Correct. A parietal lesion gives a contralateral inferior quadrantanopia.
Bitemporal loss is a chiasm lesion.

q: As lesions move more posteriorly along the pathway, the homonymous defects become:
w: Congruity increases posteriorly: tract lesions are incongruous; occipital lesions are highly congruous.
k: Posterior = more congruous.
decode: The more POSTERIOR the lesion, the MORE CONGRUOUS the homonymous defect (fibers become better aligned toward the occipital cortex). Anterior (tract) lesions are incongruous.
ow: Correct. Posterior lesions give more congruous defects.
Retrochiasmal defects are homonymous, not monocular.
Bitemporal is a chiasm pattern, not a posterior trend.
Incongruity decreases, not increases, posteriorly.

q: An occipital cortex lesion characteristically produces a homonymous hemianopia with:
w: Occipital lesions often spare the macula (dual blood supply / large cortical representation).
k: Occipital lesion = macular sparing.
decode: An OCCIPITAL lesion gives a homonymous hemianopia with MACULAR SPARING (the macular cortex has dual blood supply). No pupil involvement, not total blindness.
ow: It is a hemianopia, not total blindness.
Bitemporal is a chiasm pattern.
Cortical lesions spare the pupil reflex.
Correct. Occipital lesions give homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing.

q: Why do cortical (post-LGB) lesions NOT affect the pupillary light reflex?
o: The pupil has a separate retina
Pupil fibers leave at the pretectum
Cortical lesions are mild by nature
The cortex drives the light reflex
w: Pupillomotor fibers leave the tract at the pretectal area, so cortical lesions spare the light reflex.
k: Pupil fibers exit at pretectum (pre-cortex).
decode: Cortical (post-LGB) lesions spare the pupil because the pupillary light-reflex fibers LEAVE the pathway at the PRETECTUM (before the cortex). So vision is lost but the reflex works.
ow: The pupil shares the same retina; that is not the reason.
Correct. Pupil fibers branch off at the pretectum, before the cortex.
Severity is not the reason cortical lesions spare the pupil.
The cortex does not drive the light reflex; the midbrain does.

q: Binasal hemianopia results from damage to:
o: Meyer's loop in the temporal lobe
w: Lateral compression of the uncrossed temporal fibers on both sides gives a binasal field loss (rare).
k: Binasal = uncrossed temporal fiber damage.
decode: Binasal hemianopia needs damage to the UNCROSSED (temporal) fibers on BOTH sides (e.g., bilateral carotid compression of the chiasm's sides). Crossing-fiber damage gives bitemporal loss instead.
ow: The occipital pole gives homonymous, not binasal, loss.
Correct. Bilateral uncrossed-fiber damage gives binasal hemianopia.
Meyer's loop gives a superior quadrantanopia.
Damaging the crossing nasal fibers gives BItemporal loss.

q: At the LGB, temporal (uncrossed) retinal fibers terminate in which layers?
w: Temporal/ipsilateral fibers go to LGB layers 2, 3, 5; nasal/crossed go to 1, 4, 6.
k: Temporal fibers → LGB 2, 3, 5.
decode: At the LGB the TEMPORAL (uncrossed) fibers terminate in layers 2, 3, and 5; the crossed (nasal) fibers go to 1, 4, 6. Match uncrossed to 2, 3, 5.
ow: They terminate in specific layers, not all six.
They do terminate in the LGB.
Correct. Uncrossed (temporal) fibers end in layers 2, 3, 5.
Layers 1, 4, 6 receive the CROSSED (nasal) fibers.

q: The white band of myelinated fibers within area 17 is the:
w: The striae of Gennari (geniculocalcarine fibers) give the primary visual cortex its 'striate' name.
k: Striae of Gennari = area 17 marker.
decode: The white myelinated band within area 17 (which names the striate cortex) is the stria (striae) of Gennari. Not the optic radiation, lamina cribrosa, or Meyer's loop.
ow: The optic radiation is the pathway to the cortex, not this band.
Correct. The stria of Gennari is the white band in area 17.
The lamina cribrosa is at the optic nerve head.
Meyer's loop is part of the temporal radiation.

q: The optic vesicle arises from the:
w: The optic vesicle evaginates from the diencephalon; it then induces the surface ectoderm to form the lens.
k: Optic vesicle = diencephalon.
decode: The optic vesicle grows out of the DIENCEPHALON (forebrain neuroectoderm). Not neural crest, mesoderm, or surface ectoderm.
ow: Neural crest forms the sclera, choroid stroma, and more, not the vesicle.
Mesoderm forms extraocular muscles and vascular endothelium.
Surface ectoderm forms the lens and corneal epithelium.
Correct. The optic vesicle arises from the diencephalon.

q: Which major ocular structure is derived entirely from surface ectoderm?
w: The lens forms entirely from the surface-ectoderm lens placode; the cornea epithelium also comes from surface ectoderm.
k: Lens = surface ectoderm (entirely).
decode: The CRYSTALLINE LENS derives entirely from SURFACE ECTODERM (the lens placode). The retina is neuroectoderm; sclera and choroid are neural crest/mesoderm.
ow: The sclera is from neural crest and mesoderm.
The choroid is from neural crest and mesoderm.
Correct. The lens is entirely surface ectoderm.
The retina is neuroectoderm, not surface ectoderm.

q: Failure of the fetal (choroidal) fissure to close results in a coloboma located:
w: The fetal fissure lies inferonasally, so colobomas are always inferior (6 o'clock) when it fails to close (~week 7).
k: Coloboma = inferior (fetal fissure).
decode: The fetal (choroidal) fissure closes INFERIORLY, so failed closure gives an INFERO(nasal) coloboma. That inferonasal location is the tell.
ow: Colobomas from the fissure are inferior, not temporal.
The fissure is inferior, so defects are not superior.
Correct. Failed fissure closure gives an inferonasal coloboma.
The location is predictable (inferonasal), not random.

q: Which vitreous becomes the adult vitreous gel?
w: The secondary (avascular) vitreous becomes the adult gel; the primary regresses; the tertiary becomes zonules.
k: Secondary vitreous = adult gel.
decode: The SECONDARY vitreous becomes the adult vitreous gel (avascular). The primary vitreous regresses (leaving Cloquet's canal); the tertiary vitreous forms the zonules.
ow: Correct. The secondary vitreous forms the adult gel.
One of the three does form the adult gel.
The primary vitreous regresses, leaving Cloquet's canal.
The tertiary vitreous forms the zonules, not the gel.

q: The tertiary vitreous gives rise to the:
w: The tertiary vitreous forms the fibrillin-rich zonular fibers that suspend the lens.
k: Tertiary vitreous = lens zonules.
decode: The TERTIARY vitreous gives rise to the LENS ZONULES (suspensory ligament). The secondary forms the adult gel; the primary forms the hyaloid system.
ow: The adult gel comes from the secondary vitreous.
The hyaloid artery is part of the primary vitreous.
The cornea is from surface ectoderm and neural crest.
Correct. The tertiary vitreous forms the lens zonules.

q: Persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous (PHPV/PFV) presents with leukocoria because:
o: The primary vitreous fails to regress
The lens fails to form at all
w: Retained fibrovascular primary vitreous behind the lens appears as a white pupil; absence of calcium helps distinguish it from retinoblastoma.
k: PHPV = primary vitreous fails to regress → leukocoria.
decode: PHPV causes leukocoria because the PRIMARY vitreous FAILS TO REGRESS, leaving a retrolental fibrovascular mass. It is not a detachment, calcium, or absent lens.
ow: A retinal detachment is a consequence, not the core defect.
Correct. PHPV is failed regression of the primary vitreous.
Calcification suggests retinoblastoma, not PHPV.
The lens forms; the primary vitreous persists.

q: In Marfan syndrome (FBN1 mutation), the lens typically dislocates:
w: Weak fibrillin zonules in Marfan cause superotemporal lens dislocation; homocystinuria dislocates inferonasally.
k: Marfan = superior lens dislocation.
decode: Marfan (FBN1, weak zonules) dislocates the lens UP (superotemporal). Homocystinuria dislocates it DOWN. Marfan = up.
ow: Down-and-in is homocystinuria, not Marfan.
Correct. Marfan lens dislocates superiorly (up and out).
It does dislocate; ectopia lentis is a Marfan feature.
It subluxates within the zonular plane, typically up, not into the vitreous.

q: Aniridia is most associated with a mutation in which gene?
w: PAX6 is a master eye-development gene; its mutation causes aniridia.
k: Aniridia = PAX6 mutation.
decode: Aniridia is a PAX6 gene disorder (a master eye-development gene). FBN1 is Marfan, RB1 is retinoblastoma, COL4A1 is a vascular collagen disorder.
ow: FBN1 causes Marfan syndrome, not aniridia.
Correct. Aniridia is a PAX6 mutation.
RB1 causes retinoblastoma.
COL4A1 causes a collagen/vascular disorder, not aniridia.

q: The corneal stroma and endothelium are derived from:
w: Neural crest cells form the corneal stroma and endothelium; the corneal epithelium comes from surface ectoderm.
k: Corneal stroma + endothelium = neural crest.
decode: The corneal stroma and endothelium come from NEURAL CREST cells. Only the corneal EPITHELIUM is surface ectoderm; the retina is neuroectoderm.
ow: Mesoderm forms muscles and vascular endothelium, not corneal stroma.
Neuroectoderm forms the retina, not the corneal stroma.
Surface ectoderm forms the corneal epithelium, not the stroma/endothelium.
Correct. Corneal stroma and endothelium are neural crest.

q: The retina develops from the:
w: The two walls of the optic cup (neuroectoderm) form the neurosensory retina and the RPE.
k: Retina = neuroectoderm (optic cup).
decode: The retina develops from NEUROECTODERM (optic cup, from the diencephalon). Not mesoderm, neural crest, or surface ectoderm.
ow: Mesoderm forms muscles and vessels, not the retina.
Correct. The retina is neuroectoderm.
Neural crest forms sclera and corneal stroma, not the retina.
Surface ectoderm forms the lens and corneal epithelium.

q: The extraocular muscles are derived from:
w: The EOMs arise from mesoderm; most other orbital connective tissue is neural crest.
k: EOMs = mesoderm.
decode: The extraocular muscles derive from MESODERM (mesenchyme). Not surface ectoderm, neural crest, or endoderm.
ow: Surface ectoderm forms the lens, not muscles.
Neural crest forms connective tissue, not the muscle fibers.
Correct. The extraocular muscles are mesoderm.
Endoderm forms gut lining, not eye muscles.

q: The hyaloid artery normally fully regresses by:
w: The hyaloid system regresses by about week 36 (birth); its canal remnant is Cloquet's canal, and the Mittendorf dot is a posterior-capsule remnant.
k: Hyaloid artery regresses by birth (~week 36).
decode: The hyaloid artery normally regresses fully by about WEEK 36 / birth. A persistent remnant after birth is abnormal (PHPV/Bergmeister's).
ow: It should be gone by birth, not persisting to age 1.
Week 7 is far too early; the artery is still active.
Correct. The hyaloid artery regresses by about week 36 / birth.
Week 20 is too early for full regression.

q: The thinnest motor cranial nerve is:
w: CN4 is both the thinnest motor cranial nerve and the one with the longest intracranial course, which is why it is so vulnerable to closed head trauma.
k: CN4 = thinnest motor nerve, longest course.
decode: The thinnest motor cranial nerve is CN4 (trochlear), with the fewest axons and the longest course. That makes it easily damaged by trauma.
ow: CN7 is a larger nerve than CN4.
CN6 is thicker than CN4.
CN3 is a large motor nerve, not the thinnest.
Correct. CN4 is the thinnest motor cranial nerve.

q: CN7 exits the skull through which foramen?
w: The facial nerve leaves the skull at the stylomastoid foramen before branching over the face to supply the orbicularis oculi.
k: CN7 exits at the stylomastoid foramen.
decode: CN7 (facial) exits the skull through the STYLOMASTOID foramen. The orbital fissures and optic canal transmit eye-related nerves and vessels.
ow: The superior orbital fissure transmits CN3, 4, V1, 6, not CN7.
Correct. CN7 exits through the stylomastoid foramen.
The optic canal transmits CN2 and the ophthalmic artery.
Foramen rotundum transmits V2, not CN7.

q: Besides CN2, the optic canal also transmits the:
w: The optic canal carries CN2, the ophthalmic artery, and sympathetic fibers. The superior ophthalmic vein and the V1 branches travel through the superior orbital fissure instead.
k: Optic canal = CN2 + ophthalmic artery + sympathetics.
decode: Besides CN2, the OPTIC CANAL also transmits the OPHTHALMIC ARTERY. The lacrimal, frontal nerves and the superior ophthalmic vein use the superior orbital fissure.
ow: Correct. The ophthalmic artery runs with CN2 in the optic canal.
The lacrimal nerve uses the superior orbital fissure.
The frontal nerve uses the superior orbital fissure.
The superior ophthalmic vein uses the superior orbital fissure.

q: How many paired bones make up the skull?
w: Eight paired bones: palatine, parietal, temporal, inferior nasal concha, maxilla, nasal, zygoma, and lacrimal.
k: 8 paired skull bones.
decode: There are 8 PAIRED skull bones. The orbit itself involves 7 bones, but the paired-skull-bone count is 8.
ow: Fewer than the eight paired skull bones.
Seven is the orbital bone count, not paired skull bones.
Correct. Eight paired bones make up the skull.
One more than the eight paired skull bones.

q: Which cranial nerve supplies the superior oblique of the opposite side?
w: CN4 decussates completely in the anterior medullary velum, so each trochlear nucleus drives the contralateral superior oblique.
k: CN4 = crossed, supplies contralateral SO.
decode: CN4 supplies the superior oblique of the OPPOSITE side (it fully decussates). CN6 is the lateral rectus; CN3 runs the rest; CN7 is facial.
ow: Correct. CN4 innervates the contralateral superior oblique.
CN6 runs the lateral rectus, uncrossed.
CN7 is facial motor, not an eye-muscle nerve.
CN3 runs most eye muscles, ipsilaterally.

q: The thickest wall of the orbit is the:
w: The lateral wall, formed by the greater wing of the sphenoid and the zygomatic bone, is the thickest and strongest. The medial wall is the thinnest.
k: Lateral wall thickest; medial thinnest.
decode: The THICKEST orbital wall is the LATERAL wall (zygomatic + greater wing of sphenoid), the most protective. The medial wall (lamina papyracea) is thinnest.
ow: The roof is thinner than the lateral wall.
The floor is thin (blowout site), not thickest.
The medial wall is the THINNEST, not thickest.
Correct. The lateral wall is the thickest, most protective wall.

q: The primary action of the inferior oblique is:
w: The IO's primary action is extorsion, with elevation secondary and abduction tertiary. The SO is its mirror image: intorsion primary, depression secondary.
k: IO primary = extorsion; SO primary = intorsion.
decode: The inferior oblique's PRIMARY action is EXTORSION (it also elevates and abducts). Obliques torsion first; the inferior one extorts.
ow: Correct. The inferior oblique's primary action is extorsion.
Intorsion is the SUPERIOR oblique's primary action.
Abduction is a secondary IO action, not primary.
Depression is a superior oblique action, not the inferior oblique.

q: Which rectus muscle inserts farthest from the limbus?
w: By the Spiral of Tillaux the SR inserts farthest at 7.7 mm; the MR is nearest at 5.5 mm and is the strongest rectus.
k: SR farthest (7.7 mm); MR nearest (5.5 mm).
decode: By the spiral of Tillaux, the SUPERIOR rectus inserts farthest from the limbus (~7.7 mm); the medial rectus is closest. Superior = farthest.
ow: The medial rectus inserts closest to the limbus.
The inferior rectus is closer than the superior.
Correct. The superior rectus inserts farthest from the limbus.
The lateral rectus is intermediate, not farthest.

q: The three layers of orbital fascia, from outside in, are:
w: Periorbita lines the bone, the orbital septum forms the anterior barrier, and Tenon's capsule envelops the globe.
k: Periorbita → septum → Tenon's.
decode: From outside in, the orbital fascial layers run periorbita, then the orbital septum, then Tenon's capsule around the globe. Start at the bony lining (periorbita).
ow: Periorbita comes first (outermost), before Tenon's.
Periorbita is outermost, then septum, then Tenon's.
Correct. Periorbita, then orbital septum, then Tenon's capsule.
The periorbita, not the septum, is outermost.

q: To prevent sympathetic ophthalmia, a severely traumatized blind eye should be enucleated within:
w: Enucleating the injured eye within about 2 weeks removes the uveal antigen before the fellow eye can mount granulomatous uveitis.
k: Enucleate within 2 weeks to prevent sympathetic ophthalmia.
decode: To prevent sympathetic ophthalmia, a blind, severely injured eye should be enucleated within about 2 WEEKS (before the autoimmune reaction sensitizes the fellow eye). Not 48 hours or many months.
ow: Correct. Enucleate within about 2 weeks to prevent sympathetic ophthalmia.
Six months is too late to reliably prevent it.
48 hours is stricter than the standard 2-week window.
One year is far too late.

q: The superior ophthalmic vein enters the orbit through the:
w: The SOF transmits CN3, CN4, CN6, the V1 branches (frontal, lacrimal, nasociliary), and the superior ophthalmic vein.
k: Superior ophthalmic vein = SOF.
decode: The superior ophthalmic vein enters through the SUPERIOR ORBITAL FISSURE (with CN3, 4, V1, 6). Not the inferior fissure, rotundum, or optic canal.
ow: Correct. The superior ophthalmic vein uses the superior orbital fissure.
The inferior orbital fissure carries the inferior ophthalmic vein and V2 branches.
Foramen rotundum transmits V2, not the vein.
The optic canal carries CN2 and the ophthalmic artery.

q: The dilator pupillae is innervated by:
w: The dilator is sympathetic; the sphincter is parasympathetic via CN3 and the short ciliary nerves. Losing the sympathetic supply gives the miosis of Horner's.
k: Dilator = sympathetic; sphincter = CN3.
decode: The DILATOR pupillae is SYMPATHETIC (mydriasis). The sphincter is parasympathetic CN3. Dilator = sympathetic.
ow: Parasympathetic CN3 runs the sphincter, not the dilator.
Correct. The dilator pupillae is sympathetically innervated.
CN7 does not run the iris dilator.
CN5 is sensory, not the dilator's nerve.

q: The safest surgical entry point into the eye through the ciliary body is the:
w: The pars plana is the least vascular part of the ciliary body, so entry there minimizes bleeding. The pars plicata is where aqueous is made and is highly vascular.
k: Pars plana = least vascular = surgical entry.
decode: The safe surgical entry through the ciliary body is the PARS PLANA (flat, avascular, no retina). The pars plicata (ciliary processes) and iris root are vascular and unsafe.
ow: The ciliary processes are vascular; not a safe entry.
The iris root is anterior and vascular.
Correct. The pars plana is the safe surgical entry.
The pars plicata has ciliary processes; not safe.

q: Which layer supplies the outer retina and carries most of the eye's blood flow?
w: The choriocapillaris carries 65–85% of ocular blood flow and nourishes the outer retina, including the photoreceptors. The central retinal artery serves only the inner retina.
k: Choriocapillaris = outer retina, most blood flow.
decode: The CHORIOCAPILLARIS supplies the outer retina and carries the eye's HIGHEST blood flow (per gram, the choroid is the busiest). Bruch's and RPE are non-vascular layers.
ow: Bruch's membrane is a barrier, not a blood supply.
Correct. The choriocapillaris feeds the outer retina and has the highest flow.
The RPE is an epithelium, not a vascular layer.
The central retinal artery feeds the inner retina, with less total flow.

q: The layer lying between the choroid and the RPE is:
w: Bruch's membrane is about 7 µm thick and separates the choriocapillaris from the RPE. Breaks in it allow choroidal neovascularization in wet AMD.
k: Bruch's membrane sits between choroid and RPE.
decode: Between the choroid and RPE lies BRUCH'S membrane. The lamina fusca is the inner scleral surface; the choriocapillaris is within the choroid.
ow: Tenon's capsule surrounds the globe externally, not this interface.
The lamina fusca is the inner sclera, not between choroid and RPE.
The choriocapillaris is part of the choroid, external to Bruch's.
Correct. Bruch's membrane lies between choroid and RPE.

q: Argyll-Robertson pupils are classically caused by:
w: Argyll-Robertson pupils come from a pretectal lesion in neurosyphilis or tabes dorsalis: small, irregular pupils that accommodate but do not react to light.
k: Argyll-Robertson = neurosyphilis, pretectal.
decode: Argyll-Robertson pupils (small, irregular, light-near dissociation) are classically caused by NEUROSYPHILIS. Not aneurysm, ciliary ganglion, or sympathetic injury.
ow: A PCoM aneurysm causes a CN3 palsy with a blown pupil.
Ciliary ganglion damage causes Adie's tonic pupil.
Sympathetic injury causes Horner's, not Argyll-Robertson.
Correct. Argyll-Robertson pupils are classic for neurosyphilis.

q: Adie's tonic pupil results from damage to the:
w: Adie's follows damage to the ciliary ganglion or short ciliary nerves. It is benign, and the denervated sphincter becomes supersensitive to dilute pilocarpine.
k: Adie's = ciliary ganglion, benign.
decode: Adie's tonic pupil results from CILIARY GANGLION damage (postganglionic parasympathetic). Not the pretectal or Edinger-Westphal nuclei, nor the sympathetic ganglion.
ow: The pretectal nucleus is the light-reflex relay, not Adie's site.
Correct. Adie's pupil is ciliary ganglion damage.
Edinger-Westphal is the preganglionic parasympathetic nucleus, not the lesion site.
The superior cervical ganglion is sympathetic (Horner's).

q: The rate of aqueous humor production is about:
w: Aqueous is produced at roughly 2 µL/min and turns over the anterior chamber about every 100 minutes.
k: Aqueous production = 2 µL/min.
decode: Aqueous is produced at about 2 microliters per minute. 25 and 10 are too fast; 0.2 is too slow.
ow: 25 microliters per minute is far too fast.
Correct. Aqueous production is about 2 microliters per minute.
0.2 is ten times too slow.
10 microliters per minute is too fast.

q: What proportion of aqueous leaves by the trabecular route?
w: About 80% drains conventionally through the trabecular meshwork into Schlemm's canal; the remaining 20% leaves by the uveoscleral route, which prostaglandin drugs exploit.
k: Trabecular 80%; uveoscleral 20%.
decode: About 80% of aqueous leaves by the TRABECULAR (conventional) route; ~20% is uveoscleral. Trabecular = the larger share.
ow: 20% is the uveoscleral share.
50% understates the trabecular route.
Correct. About 80% of outflow is trabecular.
95% overstates it; some outflow is uveoscleral.

q: Episcleral venous pressure sets the floor for IOP at about:
w: Aqueous drains into the episcleral veins, so IOP cannot fall below their pressure of roughly 10 mmHg. Normal IOP runs 10–21 mmHg.
k: Episcleral venous pressure ~10 mmHg = IOP floor.
decode: Episcleral venous pressure sets the IOP FLOOR at about 8-10 mmHg (aqueous cannot drain below it). Not 2, 21, or 30.
ow: 21 is the upper normal limit, not the floor.
30 is elevated, not the venous-pressure floor.
2 is far below episcleral venous pressure.
Correct. Episcleral venous pressure floors IOP near 10 mmHg.

q: The volume of the vitreous is approximately:
w: The vitreous is about 4.5 mL, roughly 80% of the globe's volume, and is 98.5% water held as a gel by hyaluronic acid.
k: Vitreous = 4.5 mL, 98.5% water.
decode: The vitreous volume is about 4.5 mL, roughly 80% of the globe. Not 0.25, 1.5, or 9 mL.
ow: 1.5 mL is too small for the vitreous cavity.
0.25 mL is closer to the anterior chamber volume.
Correct. The vitreous is about 4.5 mL.
9 mL is larger than the whole eye.

q: Which molecule gives the vitreous its gel character?
w: Hyaluronic acid binds water and holds the vitreous as a gel. As it degrades with age the gel liquefies, producing syneresis and posterior vitreous detachment.
k: Hyaluronic acid = vitreous gel.
decode: HYALURONIC ACID (hyaluronan) gives the vitreous its gel character, holding water within a collagen framework. Not collagen IV, fibrillin, or albumin.
ow: Collagen IV is a basement-membrane collagen, not the gel-former.
Fibrillin forms zonules, not the vitreous gel.
Correct. Hyaluronic acid gives the vitreous its gel character.
Albumin is a plasma protein, not the gel matrix.

q: The thickest basement membrane in the human body is the:
w: The anterior lens capsule is about 15 µm thick, the thickest basement membrane in the body. The posterior capsule is the thinnest at 2.2 µm, which is why it is so easily ruptured in surgery.
k: Anterior lens capsule = thickest BM (15 µm).
decode: The thickest basement membrane in the body is the ANTERIOR LENS CAPSULE. Bruch's, Descemet's, and the posterior capsule are all thinner.
ow: Correct. The anterior lens capsule is the thickest basement membrane.
Bruch's membrane is thinner than the anterior capsule.
The posterior capsule is much thinner than the anterior.
Descemet's is a thick membrane but not the thickest.

q: At rest, the crystalline lens contributes approximately how much refractive power?
w: The unaccommodated lens supplies 10–15 D. The cornea is the stronger element at about 43 D, but only the lens can change its power.
k: Lens at rest = 10–15 D; cornea = 43 D.
decode: At rest the lens contributes about 10-15 D (the cornea does ~43 D). Not 20-25 or 43.
ow: Correct. The resting lens contributes about 10-15 D.
20-25 D overstates the resting lens power.
43 D is the CORNEA's power, not the lens.
3-5 D is far too low for the lens.

q: Cloquet's canal is a remnant of the:
w: Cloquet's (the hyaloid) canal runs from the disc to the posterior lens, marking the path of the regressed hyaloid artery. Its dilated end at the disc is the area of Martegiani.
k: Cloquet's canal = hyaloid artery remnant.
decode: Cloquet's canal is the remnant of the HYALOID ARTERY through the vitreous. Not the optic stalk, neural crest, or lens fibers.
ow: The optic stalk becomes the optic nerve, not Cloquet's canal.
Correct. Cloquet's canal is the hyaloid artery remnant.
Neural crest forms connective tissue, not this canal.
Primary lens fibers form the embryonic lens nucleus.

q: Muscae volitantes (floaters) represent:
w: Muscae volitantes are vitreous floaters left over from the embryonic hyaloid vascular system, seen as drifting specks against a bright background.
k: Muscae volitantes = hyaloid remnants.
decode: Muscae volitantes (small floaters) are HYALOID SYSTEM remnants in the vitreous. Not RPE migration, lens opacities, or corneal deposits.
ow: RPE migration is a retinal change, not these floaters.
Cortical lens opacities are cataract, not vitreous floaters.
Corneal deposits are anterior, not vitreous floaters.
Correct. Muscae volitantes are hyaloid remnants in the vitreous.

q: The crystalline lens is avascular because:
o: Vessels would obstruct the optical path
Blood vessels cannot cross a capsule
w: Any vessel crossing the lens would scatter light and block the visual axis, so the lens is nourished entirely by aqueous instead.
k: Lens avascular to keep the optical path clear.
decode: The lens is avascular because vessels would OBSTRUCT THE OPTICAL PATH (scatter light). It is not that vessels cannot cross a capsule or that it lacks metabolism.
ow: Correct. Vessels would block the optical path, so the lens stays clear.
Vessels could in principle enter; the reason is optical clarity.
The lens is surface ectoderm, not mesoderm, and that is not the reason.
The lens does have metabolic needs, met by aqueous.

q: During accommodation, the ciliary muscle:
