w: Ciliary contraction pulls the ring forward and inward, which reduces its diameter, slackens the zonules, and lets the elastic lens round up. This is the step presbyopia defeats.
k: Ciliary contracts → zonules slacken → lens rounds.
decode: In accommodation the ciliary muscle CONTRACTS and SLACKENS the zonules, letting the lens round up for near. Not relax, and not tighten.
ow: The muscle contracts, not relaxes, during accommodation.
Contraction slackens (not tightens) the zonules.
The muscle contracts; it does not relax here.
Correct. Ciliary contraction slackens the zonules for near focus.

q: The sphincter pupillae lies in which zone of the iris?
w: The sphincter sits centrally in the pupillary zone; the dilator lies peripherally in the ciliary zone. The collarette marks the boundary between the two.
k: Sphincter = pupillary zone; dilator = ciliary zone.
decode: The sphincter pupillae sits in the PUPILLARY zone (inner ring near the pupil). The dilator is in the ciliary zone.
ow: The iris root is peripheral, not the sphincter's zone.
The collarette divides the zones; the sphincter is in the pupillary zone.
The ciliary zone holds the dilator, not the sphincter.
Correct. The sphincter pupillae lies in the pupillary zone.

q: The choroid is thinnest at which location?
w: The choroid runs about 0.25 mm at the posterior pole and thins to roughly 0.10 mm anteriorly.
k: Choroid: 0.25 mm posteriorly, 0.10 mm anteriorly.
decode: The choroid is THINNEST anteriorly near the ora serrata and thickest at the posterior pole. Anterior = thinnest.
ow: The macula (posterior pole) is where the choroid is thickest.
Correct. The choroid is thinnest anteriorly near the ora.
The disc margin is not the thinnest choroid point.
The posterior pole is the thickest, not thinnest.

q: Which pupil abnormality is a benign peripheral neuropathy?
w: Adie's is a benign peripheral lesion of the ciliary ganglion. Argyll-Robertson is central, from neurosyphilis and tabes dorsalis, and is anything but benign.
k: Adie's benign peripheral; Argyll-Robertson central syphilis.
decode: Adie's tonic pupil is a BENIGN peripheral (postganglionic parasympathetic) neuropathy. Horner's, Argyll-Robertson, and Marcus Gunn point to more concerning central/systemic causes.
ow: Horner's may signal serious sympathetic-pathway disease.
Correct. Adie's tonic pupil is a benign peripheral neuropathy.
Argyll-Robertson points to neurosyphilis, not benign.
A Marcus Gunn pupil signals optic nerve/retinal disease.

q: Intraocular pressure is maintained principally by:
w: IOP is set by the balance of aqueous production against outflow. The vitreous contributes to globe shape but plays no part in IOP dynamics.
k: IOP = aqueous production vs outflow, not vitreous.
decode: IOP is maintained principally by the BALANCE of aqueous PRODUCTION and OUTFLOW. The vitreous, choroidal volume, and sclera contribute little to moment-to-moment IOP.
ow: The vitreous is a fixed volume, not the IOP regulator.
Choroidal blood volume causes only minor fluctuations.
Correct. IOP is set by aqueous production versus outflow.
Scleral rigidity affects measurement, not the set point.

q: Comparing the lens surfaces, the posterior surface is:
w: The posterior lens surface has a 6 mm radius and the anterior 10 mm, so the posterior is steeper and contributes more refractive power. Greater curvature means more power.
k: Posterior lens 6 mm (steeper); anterior 10 mm.
decode: The POSTERIOR lens surface is MORE curved, radius about 6 mm (the anterior is flatter, ~10 mm). Steeper back surface.
ow: Correct. The posterior surface is more curved, radius about 6 mm.
The posterior surface is curved, not flat.
A ~10 mm radius (flatter) is the anterior surface.
The two surfaces are not equal; the back is steeper.

q: The THICKEST part of the retina is the:
w: The parafovea is thickest because ganglion cells are displaced there, piled aside to clear the foveal light path. The foveola itself is the thinnest retina.
k: Parafovea thickest; foveola thinnest.
decode: The retina is THICKEST at the PARAFOVEA (heaped ganglion cells around the fovea). The foveola is thinnest.
ow: The fovea is a depression, thinner than the parafovea.
The foveola is the thinnest point.
Correct. The parafovea is the thickest retina.
The optic disc is exiting fibers, not thickest retina.

q: In a retinal detachment, the separation occurs between the:
w: Detachment splits the neurosensory retina from the RPE at the old optic-cup potential space. The RPE-Bruch's bond is firm and does not give way.
k: RD separates photoreceptors from RPE.
decode: A retinal detachment separates the PHOTORECEPTORS from the RPE (the old embryonic cleft). Not RPE-Bruch's or choroid-sclera.
ow: Correct. Detachment separates photoreceptors from the RPE.
RPE-Bruch's separation is a pigment epithelial detachment.
Vitreous-ILM separation is a posterior vitreous detachment.
Choroid-sclera separation is a choroidal detachment.

q: Retinal disease characteristically presents as painless vision loss because the retina has no:
w: The retina carries no nociceptive fibers, so disease progresses without warning pain. That silence is exactly why retinal disease is so often caught late.
k: Retina has no pain fibers = painless loss.
decode: Retinal disease is painless because the retina has no PAIN fibers. It does have blood supply, glia, and (partly) myelin behind the lamina.
ow: The retina is unmyelinated in front of the lamina, but that is not why it is painless.
The retina has glial (Muller) support.
The retina has a blood supply.
Correct. The retina has no pain fibers, so disease is painless.

q: The inner retinal layers are supplied by the:
w: The CRA and its four branches feed the inner retina; the choriocapillaris supplies only the outer retina, the RPE and photoreceptors. This split is why a CRAO spares the fovea via the cilioretinal artery in some eyes.
k: CRA = inner retina; choriocapillaris = outer retina.
decode: The INNER retina is fed by the CENTRAL RETINAL ARTERY; the outer retina by the choriocapillaris. Inner = central retinal artery.
ow: Correct. The central retinal artery supplies the inner retina.
The ophthalmic VEIN drains blood, it does not supply the retina.
The ciliary arteries supply the uvea and outer retina.
The choriocapillaris supplies the OUTER retina.

q: Congruity of a homonymous field defect becomes complete:
w: Congruity increases the further back the lesion. Optic tract lesions are post-chiasmal yet incongruous; only at the LGB and beyond do the defects match exactly.
k: The further back the lesion, the more congruous.
decode: Homonymous defects become fully CONGRUOUS at the LGB and BEYOND (occipital). Anterior (tract) lesions are incongruous. Congruity = posterior.
ow: Correct. Congruity becomes complete at the LGB and beyond.
The chiasm gives bitemporal, not homonymous congruous, loss.
The optic tract gives INCONGRUOUS defects.
The optic nerve gives monocular, not homonymous, loss.

q: A patient with bitemporal hemianopia retains:
w: Bitemporal hemianopia knocks out the temporal fields but preserves nasal fields and central vision, so acuity can stay 20/20 while the patient collides with door frames.
k: Bitemporal hemianopia spares nasal + central vision.
decode: Bitemporal hemianopia loses both TEMPORAL fields, so the patient RETAINS the CENTRAL and NASAL fields. Not temporal-only or no vision.
ow: Temporal fields are the ones LOST, not retained.
Superior loss is a quadrant pattern, not bitemporal.
Correct. Bitemporal hemianopia retains central and nasal fields.
Useful central vision remains.

q: Wernicke's hemianopic pupil occurs only with a lesion of the:
w: Wernicke's pupil belongs to optic tract lesions. Cortical lesions spare the light reflex entirely, because pupillary fibers leave at the pretectum before the cortex.
k: Wernicke's pupil = optic tract lesion only.
decode: Wernicke's hemianopic pupil (no pupil response to light on the blind hemiretina) occurs only with an OPTIC TRACT lesion, before pupil fibers leave at the pretectum. Occipital and radiation lesions spare the pupil.
ow: Occipital lesions spare the pupil reflex entirely.
The chiasm gives bitemporal loss, not this pupil sign.
Correct. Wernicke's hemianopic pupil localizes to the optic tract.
Radiation lesions are post-pretectal and spare the pupil.

q: The crystalline lens derives from:
w: The lens comes entirely from surface ectoderm via the lens placode, the only major ocular structure with that origin. The retina is neuroectoderm; the corneal stroma and endothelium are neural crest.
k: Lens = surface ectoderm (unique).
decode: The crystalline lens derives from SURFACE ECTODERM (lens placode). Not neural crest, neuroectoderm, or mesoderm.
ow: Correct. The lens is surface ectoderm.
Neural crest forms sclera and corneal stroma.
Neuroectoderm forms the retina.
Mesoderm forms muscles and vessels.

q: The corneal stroma and endothelium derive from:
w: Neural crest cells give rise to the corneal stroma and endothelium, plus the trabecular meshwork and much of the sclera. Only the corneal epithelium is surface ectoderm.
k: Corneal stroma + endothelium = neural crest.
decode: The corneal stroma and endothelium derive from NEURAL CREST. Only the corneal epithelium is surface ectoderm.
ow: Surface ectoderm forms the corneal EPITHELIUM, not stroma/endothelium.
Endoderm forms gut lining, not cornea.
Neuroectoderm forms the retina, not corneal stroma.
Correct. The corneal stroma and endothelium are neural crest.

q: The adult vitreous gel develops from the:
w: The secondary vitreous becomes the adult gel. The primary vitreous regresses, leaving only Cloquet's canal, and the tertiary vitreous becomes the lens zonules.
k: Secondary = adult gel; tertiary = zonules; primary = Cloquet's.
decode: The adult vitreous gel forms from the SECONDARY vitreous. The primary regresses (Cloquet's canal); the tertiary forms zonules.
ow: The hyaloid artery is part of the primary vitreous.
The primary vitreous regresses, leaving Cloquet's canal.
The tertiary vitreous forms the zonules.
Correct. The secondary vitreous forms the adult gel.

q: An iris coloboma is always located:
w: The fetal fissure lies on the inferior surface of the optic cup, so failure of closure always produces an inferior, keyhole-shaped defect.
k: Coloboma always inferior (6 o'clock fetal fissure).
decode: An iris coloboma sits INFERIORLY at 6 o'clock, because the fetal fissure closes inferiorly. That fixed 6 o'clock location is the tell (a 'keyhole' pupil).
ow: The fissure is inferior, so colobomas are not at 12 o'clock.
Correct. Fetal fissure closure is inferior, so the coloboma is at 6 o'clock.
The location is predictable (inferior), not random.
Not temporal; the fissure is inferior.

q: A 58-year-old hypertensive patient wakes up with right-sided ptosis, right eye turned outward and downward, and pupil 7mm and non-reactive. What is the diagnosis and what does the pupil finding suggest?
w: Complete right CN3 palsy presents with: ptosis (LPS paralyzed), eye down and out (SR/IR/MR paralyzed; unopposed LR + SO), dilated non-reactive pupil (sphincter pupillae paralyzed). The KEY finding is the dilated, non-reactive pupil — parasympathetic pupillomotor fibers run on the outside surface of CN3. External compression (aneurysm of the posterior communicating artery) preferentially affects these outer fibers FIRST, causing early pupil involvement. Ischemic CN3 palsy (diabetes, hypertension) affects the inner motor fibers first while sparing the outer pupillomotor fibers. Pupil-involving CN3 palsy = surgical emergency until neuroimaging rules out aneurysm. CN6 palsy causes esotropia, not the down-and-out eye. CN4 palsy causes hypertropia/head tilt, not ptosis.
k: Complete right CN3 palsy presents with: ptosis (LPS paralyzed), eye down and out (SR/IR/MR paralyzed…
decode: Ptosis + eye DOWN-AND-OUT + a 7 mm NON-REACTIVE (blown) pupil is a CN3 palsy, and the pupil involvement flags COMPRESSION (aneurysm/mass), not ischemia. Ischemic CN3 spares the pupil.
ow: CN4 palsy gives vertical diplopia, not a down-and-out blown pupil.
CN6 palsy gives an adducted eye and horizontal diplopia.
Correct. Pupil-involving CN3 palsy is compressive until proven otherwise.
Ischemic CN3 palsy SPARES the pupil, so a blown pupil argues against it.

q: A child presents with preseptal eyelid swelling, proptosis, restricted eye movement, and fever. What is the most likely source of infection based on anatomy?
w: Orbital cellulitis in children most commonly originates from the ethmoidal sinus. The medial orbital wall (lamina papyracea of the ethmoid) is extremely thin and directly adjacent to the ethmoidal air cells. Bacterial sinusitis erodes through this wall, spreading infection into the orbit. The presentation — preseptal and postseptal involvement, proptosis, restricted EOM, fever — is the classic orbital cellulitis picture. The sphenoidal sinus is posterior to the orbit and relates to CN2 (retrobulbar neuritis), not direct orbital spread. The maxillary sinus relates to the orbital floor (blowout fractures). The frontal sinus relates to the orbital roof.
k: Orbital cellulitis in children most commonly originates from the ethmoidal sinus.
decode: Child + eyelid swelling + proptosis + restricted motility + fever is orbital cellulitis, and by anatomy the source is the adjacent ETHMOID sinus (thin lamina papyracea). Pick the ethmoid.
ow: The frontal sinus is a less common source.
The sphenoid is deeper and less commonly the source.
The maxillary sinus is below, a less common source.
Correct. The ethmoid sinus is the usual source via the thin medial wall.

q: A 45-year-old patient presents with vertical diplopia that worsens when looking down-and-inward. He tilts his head toward his left shoulder when reading. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
w: CN4 (trochlear) innervates the superior oblique. The SO's primary action is intorsion, secondary is depression. When it fails, the eye cannot depress or intort — this causes vertical diplopia worse on downgaze and in adduction (looking down-inward). The patient compensates by tilting the head toward the opposite shoulder (here, left), which is the classic Bielschowsky head tilt. A CN3 palsy would cause a larger picture — ptosis, dilated pupil, and the eye would be down and out. CN6 palsy causes horizontal diplopia (esotropia), not vertical.
k: CN4 (trochlear) innervates the superior oblique.
decode: Vertical diplopia worse on DOWN-AND-IN gaze with a head tilt AWAY (to the left shoulder) is a RIGHT CN4 (superior oblique) palsy. Head tilt away from the affected side is the Bielschowsky clue.
ow: A left CN3 palsy gives ptosis and a down-and-out eye, not this.
Correct. Right CN4 palsy: worse on down-and-in, head tilt to the opposite shoulder.
A right CN3 palsy would give ptosis and pupil signs.
A left CN6 palsy gives horizontal, not vertical, diplopia.

q: Which of the following correctly lists the contents of the superior orbital fissure?
o: CN3, CN4, CN6, superior ophthalmic vein
CN2, CN3, CN4, CN6, ophthalmic artery
w: The SOF carries CN3 (oculomotor), CN4 (trochlear), CN5-ophthalmic division (via its branches: frontal, lacrimal, nasociliary), CN6 (abducens), and the superior ophthalmic vein. CN2 and the ophthalmic artery pass through the optic canal — not the SOF. The inferior orbital fissure carries CN5 maxillary division and the infraorbital artery.
k: The SOF carries CN3 (oculomotor), CN4 (trochlear), CN5-ophthalmic division (via its branches: frontal…
decode: The superior orbital fissure carries CN3, CN4, CN6, V1 branches, and the superior ophthalmic vein, but NOT CN2 or the ophthalmic artery (those use the optic canal). Pick the option without CN2/artery.
ow: CN2 and the ophthalmic artery use the optic canal, not the fissure.
Correct. CN3, 4, 6 and the superior ophthalmic vein pass the fissure.
CN2 and the ophthalmic artery are in the optic canal, not the fissure.
V2 (maxillary) and the infraorbital artery use foramen rotundum/inferior fissure.

q: A 35-year-old patient complains of chronic eye irritation, foreign body sensation, and redness worsening in the afternoon. Schirmer's test (without anesthesia) measures 18 mm bilaterally. Tear break-up time is 5 seconds. Which of the following is the most likely underlying problem?
o: Aqueous-deficient dry eye from lacrimal gland hyposecretion
Excessive tear drainage due to punctal stenosis
Lipid layer deficiency from Meibomian gland dysfunction
w: The normal Schirmer's test (18 mm — well within 10–25 mm) rules out aqueous deficiency. The short TBUT (5 seconds, normal >10 seconds) indicates the tear film is breaking up too quickly despite adequate aqueous volume. The lipid layer (from Meibomian glands) is what prevents evaporation and maintains film stability. When it is deficient, the aqueous layer evaporates rapidly and the film collapses before the next blink. This is evaporative dry eye — the most common form. Symptoms worsen in the afternoon because Meibomian gland secretions accumulate and solidify with reduced blink-driven expression over the day.
k: The normal Schirmer's test (18 mm — well within 10–25 mm) rules out aqueous deficiency.
decode: Afternoon-worsening irritation with NORMAL Schirmer (18 mm) but SHORT TBUT (5 s) is EVAPORATIVE dry eye from meibomian (lipid) dysfunction. Aqueous deficiency would drop the Schirmer.
ow: Aqueous deficiency would give a LOW Schirmer, not 18 mm.
Punctal stenosis causes overflow tearing, not a short TBUT.
Goblet cell hyperplasia is not the cause of an unstable film here.
Correct. Normal Schirmer with short TBUT is lipid-layer (meibomian) deficiency.

q: A 6-week-old infant is brought in with persistent unilateral epiphora and a mucopurulent discharge since birth. The most likely diagnosis is:
w: The nasolacrimal duct is the last segment of the lacrimal drainage system to fully open during development. In up to 20% of newborns, the valve of Hasner (at the nasal opening of the nasolacrimal duct) remains membranous at birth. Tears cannot drain, accumulate in the lacrimal sac, and become secondarily infected. This presents as persistent unilateral epiphora with mucopurulent discharge starting shortly after birth. Management is conservative (massage over lacrimal sac, topical antibiotics) — most resolve spontaneously by 12 months. Probing is performed if obstruction persists beyond that. Congenital glaucoma would present with photophobia, tearing, buphthalmos, and corneal edema — not mucopurulent discharge. Neonatal gonorrheal conjunctivitis presents in the first 2–5 days of life with severe bilateral purulent discharge, not epiphora.
k: The nasolacrimal duct is the last segment of the lacrimal drainage system to fully open during development.
decode: Unilateral epiphora with mucopurulent discharge SINCE BIRTH is congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction. Congenital glaucoma gives a cloudy enlarged cornea; gonococcal conjunctivitis is hyperacute in the first days.
ow: Congenital glaucoma gives a cloudy, enlarged cornea, not discharge.
Gonococcal conjunctivitis is hyperacute in the first days of life.
Gland agenesis causes dryness, not watering and discharge.
Correct. Discharge and epiphora since birth is nasolacrimal duct obstruction.

q: A 70-year-old patient presents with progressive, painless bilateral vision loss. Slit lamp examination shows corneal edema with a beaten-metal appearance of the endothelium on specular reflection. Central pachymetry is 680 µm bilaterally. Which of the following best explains the pathophysiology?
o: Loss of endothelial Na-K ATPase pump function leading to stromal edema
Disruption of tight junctions in the corneal epithelium
Degeneration of Bowman's membrane preventing epithelial adhesion
Failure of goblet cells to produce mucin for the tear film
w: This is Fuchs' endothelial dystrophy. The endothelium normally pumps Na+ and HCO3- out of the stroma — water follows osmotically, keeping the stroma at 75–80% water. In Fuchs', endothelial cells degenerate and are not replaced (endothelium is post-mitotic). As cell density falls below a critical threshold, the pump cannot maintain deturgescence. Water accumulates in the stroma, disrupting the regular collagen fiber spacing and causing light scatter (opacity). Pachymetry above 600 µm (normal 520–560 µm) confirms stromal swelling. The "beaten-metal" or "hammered silver" appearance on specular microscopy is the endothelial guttata — excrescences on Descemet's membrane that are pathognomonic of Fuchs'. Goblet cells, tight junctions, and Bowman's membrane are unrelated to this presentation.
k: This is Fuchs' endothelial dystrophy.
decode: Painless bilateral edema, a BEATEN-METAL endothelium, and thick pachymetry (680) is Fuchs' dystrophy: ENDOTHELIAL Na-K PUMP failure lets the stroma swell. It is not an epithelial, Bowman's, or goblet-cell problem.
ow: Correct. Endothelial pump failure causes the stromal edema.
Epithelial tight junctions are not the Fuchs' defect.
Bowman's degeneration does not cause this endothelial picture.
Goblet-cell mucin failure is a surface issue, not endothelial edema.

q: During gonioscopy, the examiner identifies a thin, white, glistening line at the most anterior portion of the trabecular meshwork. What structure is this?
w: Schwalbe's line marks the peripheral termination of Descemet's membrane and the most anterior extension of the trabecular meshwork. It appears as a thin, white, glistening line projecting slightly into the anterior chamber. The gonioscopic order from anterior to posterior is: Schwalbe's line → trabecular meshwork → scleral spur → ciliary body band → peripheral iris. Sampaolesi's line is pigment deposited along Schwalbe's line — seen in pigment dispersion syndrome and pseudoexfoliation — and would appear as a pigmented line, not a white one. The scleral spur appears as a whitish band posterior to the TM. Schlemm's canal is not normally visible unless blood-filled.
k: Schwalbe's line marks the peripheral termination of Descemet's membrane and the most anterior extension of…
decode: A thin white glistening line at the MOST ANTERIOR trabecular meshwork on gonioscopy is Schwalbe's line (end of Descemet's). Schlemm's canal, Sampaolesi's line, and the scleral spur are different landmarks.
ow: Correct. Schwalbe's line is the anterior glistening line at the meshwork.
Schlemm's canal is the drainage channel, not this surface line.
Sampaolesi's line is pigment anterior to Schwalbe's, in pigment dispersion.
The scleral spur is posterior to the meshwork.

q: A patient is asked to look at a near target. Both pupils constrict. When a bright light is shone into the right eye, neither pupil constricts, but both constrict with near gaze. The left eye shows the same pattern. Which of the following best describes this condition?
w: Argyll-Robertson pupils are pathognomonic for neurosyphilis (tabes dorsalis). The hallmark is light-near dissociation: "accommodates but does not react to light." The pretectal lesion disrupts the afferent arc of the pupillary light reflex while sparing the accommodation-convergence near reflex pathway (which travels more ventrally in the brainstem). This produces bilateral small, irregular pupils that constrict with near gaze but not with light. Bilateral Adie's is possible but would show tonic (slow) near constriction and loss of deep tendon reflexes, not the complete absence of light response. Marcus-Gunn involves a relative afferent defect — it does not cause bilateral failure of the light reflex in both eyes.
k: Argyll-Robertson pupils are pathognomonic for neurosyphilis (tabes dorsalis).
decode: Bilateral pupils that DO NOT react to light but DO constrict to near (light-near dissociation) are Argyll-Robertson pupils (neurosyphilis). Adie's is tonic and usually unilateral; Horner's still reacts to light.
ow: Adie's is a tonic pupil, usually unilateral, and does react slowly to light.
Horner's pupils still react to light.
A Marcus-Gunn pupil is an afferent defect, not light-near dissociation.
Correct. Light-near dissociation bilaterally is Argyll-Robertson (neurosyphilis).

q: During a vitreoretinal surgical procedure, the surgeon enters the eye through which of the following structures to minimize bleeding risk?
w: The pars plana is the posterior, flat, avascular portion of the ciliary body (4mm wide, extending from the ora serrata to the pars plicata). Its relative avascularity makes it the preferred and safest entry point for vitreoretinal surgery, reducing hemorrhage risk. The pars plicata (anterior 2mm, most vascular) contains the ciliary processes and is avoided. The limbus is used for anterior segment surgeries (e.g., cataract). The iris root is fragile and its incision would damage the angle and drainage structures.
k: The pars plana is the posterior, flat, avascular portion of the ciliary body (4mm wide, extending from the…
decode: Vitreoretinal entry is through the PARS PLANA (avascular, no retina) to minimize bleeding. The iris root, limbus, and pars plicata are vascular or anterior.
ow: The iris root is anterior and vascular.
Correct. The pars plana is the safe, avascular entry.
The limbus is the anterior-segment entry, not for vitreoretinal work.
The pars plicata has vascular ciliary processes.

q: A 55-year-old patient has had increasing difficulty reading. Their distance vision remains 20/20. Amplitude of accommodation measures +0.5D. Which of the following is the primary mechanism?
o: Zonule degeneration preventing transmission of ciliary muscle force
Progressive hardening of the lens nucleus reducing elastic recoil
Ciliary muscle atrophy reducing zonular tension
Posterior displacement of the lens reducing its refractive power
w: Presbyopia develops because the lens adds new fibers throughout life, compressing older fibers centrally into an increasingly hard nucleus. The nucleus loses its elasticity. Even when the ciliary muscle contracts and releases zonular tension, the stiff nucleus cannot round up sufficiently to increase power for near focus. The ciliary muscle itself remains functional in early presbyopia — the problem is purely in the lens. Zonule degeneration does not typically cause presbyopia; subluxation (e.g., Marfan's) causes different problems. Posterior lens displacement would reduce accommodation range but is not the primary mechanism of presbyopia.
k: Presbyopia develops because the lens adds new fibers throughout life, compressing older fibers centrally into…
decode: Age 55, near difficulty, distance 20/20, amplitude only +0.5 D is presbyopia: the LENS NUCLEUS HARDENS and loses elastic recoil. Not zonule, ciliary, or lens-position problems.
ow: Zonules are intact in presbyopia; the lens stiffens.
Correct. Lens nucleus hardening reduces elastic recoil.
The ciliary muscle is relatively preserved in presbyopia.
The lens does not displace in presbyopia.

q: Which of the following most accurately describes the composition of aqueous humor relative to plasma?
o: Higher ascorbic acid concentration than plasma
w: Aqueous humor is actively secreted — not just a filtrate of plasma — so certain components are concentrated above plasma levels. Ascorbic acid (vitamin C) is actively pumped into the AH at concentrations 15–20× higher than plasma. It serves as an antioxidant protecting the lens and cornea from oxidative damage. Protein content is very low (25 mg% vs. Plasma ~7000 mg%) — the blood-aqueous barrier restricts protein entry, keeping AH optically clear. Osmolarity is slightly higher than plasma (not lower). Glucose is present at about 2.5 mg% in AH — lower than plasma.
k: Aqueous humor is actively secreted — not just a filtrate of plasma — so certain components are concentrated…
decode: Aqueous has HIGHER ASCORBIC ACID than plasma (an ocular antioxidant); it has LESS protein and glucose and similar osmolarity. Ascorbate up is the tell.
ow: Aqueous osmolarity is similar to plasma, not clearly lower.
Correct. Aqueous has more ascorbic acid than plasma.
Aqueous glucose is lower than plasma.
Aqueous has far less protein than plasma.

q: A patient with advanced glaucoma retains central vision but has complete loss of peripheral visual field. Which retinal cells are most directly responsible for the peripheral field loss?
o: RPE cells at the ora serrata
Bipolar cells at the inner nuclear layer
Peripheral rods and their associated ganglion cells
w: Glaucoma damages retinal ganglion cells — specifically their axons at the lamina cribrosa where elevated IOP compresses them. The peripheral ganglion cells (associated with peripheral rods for peripheral field) are more vulnerable and lost earlier in glaucoma. This produces the classic arcuate scotoma and nasal step pattern, eventually leaving only a central island of vision (tunnel vision from surviving foveal cone-ganglion pathways). The foveal cones themselves are among the last to be affected because the foveal area has a relative abundance of ganglion cells and better vascular supply. RPE cells and bipolar cells are not the primary site of glaucomatous damage.
k: Glaucoma damages retinal ganglion cells — specifically their axons at the lamina cribrosa where elevated IOP…
decode: Glaucoma spares central vision but loses the PERIPHERY, driven by loss of PERIPHERAL rods and their GANGLION cells (ganglion axons die at the lamina). Foveal cones and RPE are not the peripheral-field cells.
ow: Foveal cones serve CENTRAL vision, which is preserved.
RPE cells are not the field-carrying neurons.
Bipolar cells relay signal but are not the primary glaucoma target.
Correct. Peripheral rods and their ganglion cells underlie the lost peripheral field.

q: On fundus examination, the optic disc measures 1.5mm and the cup measures 0.7mm in diameter. Which of the following is most accurate?
o: C/D ratio of 0.7 — very concerning for glaucomatous cupping
C/D ratio of 0.47 — borderline suspicious for glaucoma
w: C/D ratio = cup diameter ÷ disc diameter = 0.7 ÷ 1.5 = 0.47. Normal C/D is ≤0.3. A ratio of 0.47 is above normal and warrants further evaluation — IOP measurement, visual field testing, and OCT of the nerve fiber layer. It is suspicious but not necessarily diagnostic.7 would be the cup diameter, not the ratio). A C/D >0.5 with asymmetry >0.2 between the two eyes raises high concern for glaucoma.
k: C/D ratio = cup diameter ÷ disc diameter = 0.7 ÷ 1.5 = 0.47.
decode: C/D = cup diameter over disc diameter = 0.7/1.5 = 0.47, which is BORDERLINE/suspicious (above the ~0.3 normal). Compute the ratio, do not read 0.7 as the C/D.
ow: 0.7 is the cup size, not the C/D ratio (which is 0.47).
Correct. 0.7/1.5 = 0.47, borderline suspicious.
0.47 is elevated above normal, so not simply normal.
0.47 is above the normal 0.3, so not clearly within range.

q: A patient presents with sudden painless vision loss, a pale swollen retina, and a cherry-red spot at the fovea. Which vascular event explains the cherry-red spot?
o: Foveal hemorrhage from a vein occlusion
Inner retinal edema sparing the thin foveola
w: In central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO), the inner retina (supplied by the CRA) becomes ischemic and edematous — the swollen cells make the retina appear pale and opaque. However, the fovea (specifically the foveola) is extremely thin — it lacks ganglion cells and inner nuclear cells. At the foveola, the transparent inner retina is so thin that the underlying choroid (still perfused by the short posterior ciliary arteries, which are not affected by CRAO) shows through as a red color against the pale surrounding retina. This contrast creates the cherry-red spot. RPE detachment is a different pathology. Vein occlusion causes flame hemorrhages, not cherry-red spot.
k: In central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO), the inner retina (supplied by the CRA) becomes ischemic and…
decode: Sudden painless loss, a pale retina, and a cherry-red fovea is CRAO: INNER RETINAL EDEMA whitens the retina while the thin foveola (fed by choroid) still shows red. The cherry spot is spared foveola, not hemorrhage.
ow: Bare sclera is not what makes the cherry-red spot.
The cherry-red spot is not a hemorrhage; the retina is pale.
Correct. Inner retinal edema whitens the retina, sparing the thin foveola.
An RPE detachment does not produce the cherry-red spot.

q: A 45-year-old woman presents with gradual loss of her peripheral vision bilaterally. She bumps into objects on both sides. Visual field testing shows loss of both temporal fields while nasal fields are intact. MRI would most likely reveal a lesion at which location?
w: Bitemporal hemianopsia — loss of both temporal fields with preserved nasal fields — is the hallmark of a chiasmal lesion affecting the crossing (decussating) fibers. These nasal fibers carry temporal field information from both eyes; their interruption at the chiasma eliminates both temporal fields simultaneously. The most common cause in a middle-aged woman is a pituitary adenoma growing upward to compress the inferior chiasma. A right optic nerve lesion would cause right monocular blindness. A right optic tract lesion would cause left homonymous hemianopsia (not bitemporal). Occipital cortex lesion causes homonymous scotoma — not bitemporal loss.
k: Bitemporal hemianopsia — loss of both temporal fields with preserved nasal fields — is the hallmark of a…
decode: Bilateral loss of both TEMPORAL fields (bitemporal hemianopia) localizes to the OPTIC CHIASM, where the crossing nasal fibers are compressed. Nerve, tract, and occipital lesions give other patterns.
ow: An occipital lesion gives homonymous, not bitemporal, loss.
One optic nerve gives monocular loss, not bitemporal.
An optic tract lesion gives homonymous, not bitemporal, loss.
Correct. Bitemporal hemianopia localizes to the optic chiasm.

q: A 60-year-old man suffers a right-sided stroke involving the temporal lobe. Which visual field defect is most likely on examination?
o: Left homonymous hemianopsia with macular sparing
w: The inferior fibers of the right optic radiation loop through the temporal lobe (Meyer's loop) before reaching the occipital cortex. These fibers carry information from the superior visual field of the left hemifield. A right temporal lobe stroke interrupts Meyer's loop, producing a left superior quadrantanopsia — classically called "pie in the sky" (the upper-left visual field is lost). Left inferior quadrantanopsia would result from a right parietal lobe lesion (superior radiation fibers). Left homonymous hemianopsia with macular sparing is a right occipital cortex finding. Bitemporal hemianopsia requires a chiasmal lesion.
k: The inferior fibers of the right optic radiation loop through the temporal lobe (Meyer's loop) before…
decode: A right TEMPORAL lobe stroke hits Meyer's loop, giving a LEFT SUPERIOR quadrantanopia ('pie in the sky', contralateral and superior). Not a full hemianopia or inferior quadrant.
ow: A full hemianopia with macular sparing is an occipital lesion.
Correct. Right temporal (Meyer's loop) gives left superior quadrantanopia.
Inferior quadrantanopia is a parietal lesion.
Bitemporal loss is a chiasm lesion, not a temporal-lobe stroke.

q: A newborn presents with leukocoria (white pupil). On examination, a white fibrovascular mass is noted behind the lens. B-scan ultrasound shows a retrolental mass with no calcium deposits. Which embryological failure best explains this finding?
o: Failure of lens vesicle to separate from surface ectoderm
Failure of primary vitreous to regress
Failure of secondary vitreous to form
w: This is Persistent Hyperplastic Primary Vitreous (PHPV), now called Persistent Fetal Vasculature (PFV). The primary vitreous, which is vascular and contains the hyaloid artery system, normally regresses completely by birth. When it persists, the remaining fibrovascular tissue forms a white retrolental mass — leukocoria. The absence of calcium deposits distinguishes it from retinoblastoma (which often calcifies). Fetal fissure failure produces coloboma (not a retrolental mass). Lens vesicle failure would prevent lens formation. Secondary vitreous failure does not cause leukocoria.
k: This is Persistent Hyperplastic Primary Vitreous (PHPV), now called Persistent Fetal Vasculature (PFV).
decode: Leukocoria + retrolental fibrovascular mass + NO calcium is PHPV: FAILURE of the PRIMARY VITREOUS to REGRESS. Calcium would suggest retinoblastoma instead.
ow: Failed fissure closure gives a coloboma, not a retrolental mass.
Failed lens-vesicle separation gives a corneal-lens stalk, not this.
Correct. PHPV is failure of the primary vitreous to regress.
The secondary vitreous does form; the primary fails to regress.

q: A 16-year-old male with tall stature, long fingers, and arachnodactyly presents with sudden visual blur in the right eye. Slit-lamp exam shows the right lens displaced superiorly. Which of the following correctly links the genetic defect to the embryological structure affected?
o: FBN1 mutation → weak fibrillin zonules → lens dislocation
COL4A1 mutation → abnormal lens capsule → lens rupture
PAX6 mutation → failure of iris differentiation → aniridia
FBN1 mutation → weak secondary vitreous → lens dislocation
w: This is Marfan syndrome. The tertiary vitreous forms the lens zonules (suspensory ligament) from fibrillin-containing microfibrils. FBN1 encodes fibrillin-1. When fibrillin is structurally abnormal, the zonules are weak and break under normal tension. The lens dislocates — classically in the superotemporal direction. This is ectopia lentis. The secondary vitreous forms the vitreous gel, not the zonules. PAX6 mutation causes aniridia — no lens dislocation. COL4A1 mutations affect type IV collagen and cause cerebrovascular disease, not lens dislocation.
k: This is Marfan syndrome.
decode: Marfan (tall, arachnodactyly) with a superiorly dislocated lens is FBN1 -> weak FIBRILLIN ZONULES -> ectopia lentis. The zonules (not the capsule or vitreous) fail, and PAX6/COL4A1 are other genes.
ow: Correct. FBN1 weakens fibrillin zonules, dislocating the lens.
COL4A1 is a vascular collagen gene, not the Marfan capsule mechanism.
PAX6 causes aniridia, not Marfan lens dislocation.
Marfan weakens the zonules, not the secondary vitreous.

q: The lipid layer of the tear film comes mainly from the:
w: Meibomian glands supply most of the lipid, with a contribution from the glands of Zeis. Losing it gives evaporative dry eye: normal Schirmer, short TBUT.
k: Lipid layer = Meibomian (plus Zeis).
decode: The LIPID layer comes from the MEIBOMIAN glands (tarsal oil glands). Goblet cells make mucin; the lacrimal and accessory glands make aqueous.
ow: Goblet cells make the mucin layer, not lipid.
Correct. The meibomian glands make the lipid layer.
The main lacrimal gland makes aqueous, not lipid.
The glands of Krause make basal aqueous, not lipid.

q: Reflex aqueous tear secretion comes from the:
w: The main lacrimal gland handles reflex tearing under CN7 control. Basic resting secretion comes from the accessory glands of Krause and Wolfring.
k: Reflex = main lacrimal gland (CN7); basic = Krause + Wolfring.
decode: REFLEX aqueous tears come from the MAIN lacrimal gland; the accessory glands (Krause, Wolfring) supply BASAL secretion. Reflex = main gland.
ow: Meibomian glands make lipid, not reflex aqueous.
Glands of Krause supply basal, not reflex, secretion.
Glands of Wolfring supply basal secretion.
Correct. The main lacrimal gland supplies reflex aqueous tears.

q: The thinnest layer of the tear film is the:
w: Mucin is thinnest at about 0.03 µm, lipid next at 0.5 µm, and aqueous thickest at 7 µm. Thin does not mean unimportant: mucin is what lets the aqueous wet the cornea at all.
k: Mucin 0.03 µm < lipid 0.5 µm < aqueous 7 µm.
decode: The MUCIN layer is the THINNEST tear layer (innermost, anchoring the film). Aqueous is thickest; lipid is a thin outer film but mucin is thinnest.
ow: The aqueous layer is the thickest, not thinnest.
The layers are not equal; mucin is thinnest.
Correct. The mucin layer is the thinnest.
The lipid layer is thin but the mucin is thinnest.

q: CN7 reaches the lacrimal gland by which route?
w: The parasympathetic path runs greater petrosal → Vidian → pterygopalatine ganglion → lacrimal nerve. Misdirected regeneration along it produces crocodile tears.
k: CN7 → greater petrosal → Vidian → pterygopalatine → lacrimal.
decode: CN7 parasympathetic fibers reach the lacrimal gland via the GREATER (superficial) PETROSAL nerve (to the pterygopalatine ganglion). Not the ciliary, infraorbital, or nasociliary routes.
ow: The short ciliary nerves carry pupil/ciliary fibers, not lacrimal.
The infraorbital nerve is sensory (V2), not the lacrimal secretomotor route.
The nasociliary nerve is sensory, not the CN7 lacrimal route.
Correct. CN7 reaches the gland via the greater petrosal nerve.

q: A normal Schirmer's test without anesthesia measures:
w: Normal is 10–25 mm in 5 minutes without anesthesia. Under 10 mm suggests aqueous deficiency. TBUT under 10 seconds points instead to instability.
k: Schirmer normal 10–25 mm/5 min; TBUT >10 s.
decode: A normal Schirmer's WITHOUT anesthesia wets about 10-25 mm in 5 minutes. Lower values indicate aqueous deficiency; 30-40 is hypersecretion.
ow: Correct. Normal Schirmer (no anesthesia) is about 10-25 mm/5 min.
5-8 mm is low, suggesting dry eye.
2-5 mm is markedly reduced.
30-40 mm suggests reflex hypersecretion or irritation.

q: Lysozyme makes up roughly what share of tear protein?
w: Lysozyme is 21–25% of tear protein and lyses bacterial cell walls, working alongside secretory IgA and lactoferrin as the tear film's defense.
k: Lysozyme = 21–25% of tear protein.
decode: Lysozyme is about 21-25% of tear protein (a key antibacterial enzyme). Not the majority (50-80%) and not a trace 1-2%.
ow: Overstates lysozyme's share of tear protein.
Correct. Lysozyme is about 21-25% of tear protein.
Far too high for lysozyme's share.
Understates lysozyme; it is a major tear protein.

q: The six corneal layers from anterior to posterior are:
o: Epithelium → stroma → Bowman's → Dua's → Descemet's → endothelium
Epithelium → Bowman's → Dua's → stroma → Descemet's → endothelium
Epithelium → Bowman's → stroma → Dua's → Descemet's → endothelium
Endothelium → Descemet's → Dua's → stroma → Bowman's → epithelium
w: Epithelium, Bowman's, stroma, Dua's, Descemet's, endothelium. Dua's layer is the modern addition, a tough pre-Descemet's layer relevant to deep lamellar grafting.
k: Epi → Bowman's → stroma → Dua's → Descemet's → endothelium.
decode: Anterior to posterior: Epithelium, Bowman's, Stroma, Dua's, Descemet's, Endothelium. Bowman's is just under the epithelium, and Dua's sits deep, just before Descemet's.
ow: Bowman's comes before the stroma, not after it.
The stroma comes before Dua's, not after Bowman's directly.
Correct. Epithelium, Bowman's, stroma, Dua's, Descemet's, endothelium.
That is the posterior-to-anterior (reversed) order.

q: Which corneal layers CAN regenerate?
w: Epithelium regenerates from limbal stem cells, and the endothelium secretes new Descemet's. Bowman's and the endothelium itself cannot regenerate, which is why their loss is permanent.
k: Regenerate: epithelium, Descemet's. Never: Bowman's, endothelium.
decode: The EPITHELIUM regenerates readily, and DESCEMET'S can be re-secreted by the endothelium. Bowman's does NOT regenerate; the endothelium does not truly proliferate.
ow: The endothelium does not truly regenerate (cells enlarge, not divide).
Correct. Epithelium regrows and Descemet's can be re-secreted.
Bowman's does not regenerate; it scars.
Bowman's does not regenerate, and the endothelium does not proliferate.

q: The limbus is how wide, and what does it contain?
w: The limbus is a 1–2 mm transition zone holding the trabecular meshwork, Schlemm's canal and the limbal stem cells that resurface the epithelium.
k: Limbus 1–2 mm: TM, Schlemm's, stem cells.
decode: The limbus is a narrow 1-2 mm transition zone containing the trabecular meshwork and Schlemm's canal (the drainage angle). It is not 3-6 mm and does not contain the ora or ciliary body.
ow: Correct. The limbus is 1-2 mm wide with the TM and Schlemm's canal.
The ora serrata is far posterior, not in the limbus.
The ciliary body is behind the limbus, not within it.
The limbus is wider than 0.1 mm and holds the drainage structures.

q: The gonioscopic landmarks from anterior to posterior are:
o: Schwalbe's → TM → scleral spur → ciliary body → iris
TM → Schwalbe's → scleral spur → iris → ciliary body
Scleral spur → Schwalbe's → TM → ciliary body → iris
Ciliary body → iris → scleral spur → TM → Schwalbe's
w: Anterior to posterior: Schwalbe's line, trabecular meshwork, scleral spur, ciliary body band, peripheral iris. Identifying the scleral spur is what tells you the angle is open.
k: Gonioscopy: Schwalbe's → TM → spur → ciliary body → iris.
decode: Gonioscopy landmarks, anterior to posterior: Schwalbe's line, trabecular meshwork, scleral spur, ciliary body band, iris. Start at Schwalbe's (end of Descemet's).
ow: Correct. Schwalbe's, TM, scleral spur, ciliary body, iris.
Schwalbe's line comes before the TM, not after.
The scleral spur is not the most anterior landmark.
That is the reversed (posterior-to-anterior) order.

q: The foveola measures about:
w: The foveola is 0.4 mm of pure cones and is capillary-free, sitting within the 1.5 mm fovea. Being avascular, it survives a CRAO on choroidal supply, giving the cherry-red spot.
k: Foveola 0.4 mm (pure cones, avascular); fovea 1.5 mm.
decode: The foveola is about 0.4 mm across (the tiny cone-only center). Not 0.4 cm, 1.5 mm, or 3 mm.
ow: 0.4 cm is ten times too large.
Correct. The foveola is about 0.4 mm.
1.5 mm is closer to the whole fovea/disc size.
3 mm is far larger than the foveola.

q: The ora serrata lies approximately how far from the limbus?
w: The ora serrata sits about 6 mm behind the limbus, marking the anterior termination of the retina. Scleral depression is needed to view it.
k: Ora serrata ≈ 6 mm from the limbus.
decode: The ora serrata lies about 6 mm behind the limbus. 2 mm is too close; 12-24 mm is too far.
ow: 2 mm is too close; that is near the limbus itself.
Correct. The ora serrata is about 6 mm from the limbus.
12 mm is too far posterior.
24 mm is about the whole axial length, far too far.

q: The macular xanthophyll pigments are:
w: Lutein and zeaxanthin filter blue light and mop up free radicals at the macula. They are the rationale behind the AREDS2 formulation.
k: Macular pigment = lutein + zeaxanthin (AREDS2).
decode: The macular xanthophylls are LUTEIN and ZEAXANTHIN (yellow carotenoids). Erythrolabe/chlorolabe are cone opsins; melanin/lipofuscin are RPE pigments; rhodopsin/iodopsin are visual pigments.
ow: Erythrolabe and chlorolabe are cone photopigments, not xanthophylls.
Melanin and lipofuscin are RPE pigments.
Rhodopsin and iodopsin are photoreceptor visual pigments.
Correct. Lutein and zeaxanthin are the macular xanthophylls.

q: Counting from outer to inner, which is the OUTERMOST retinal layer?
w: The order runs RPE, photoreceptors, ELM, ONL, Henle's, OPL, INL, IPL, GCL, NFL, ILM. Light traverses the whole thickness to reach the photoreceptors: the retina is inverted.
k: Outer to inner: RPE → photoreceptors → … → NFL → ILM.
decode: The OUTERMOST retinal layer (nearest the choroid) is the RETINAL PIGMENT EPITHELIUM. The ILM and nerve fiber/ganglion layers are innermost (nearest the vitreous).
ow: The ganglion cell layer is inner, near the vitreous.
The nerve fiber layer is the innermost neural layer.
Correct. The RPE is the outermost retinal layer.
The internal limiting membrane is the innermost layer.

q: The optic disc sits how far above the foveola?
w: The disc lies about 3 mm nasal to the macula and 0.8 mm above the foveola, which is why the physiologic blind spot maps slightly below the horizontal midline.
k: Disc: 3 mm nasal, 0.8 mm above the foveola.
decode: The optic disc sits about 0.8 mm ABOVE the foveola (slightly superior as well as nasal). Not 3-5 mm, and not level.
ow: 3 mm is roughly the nasal distance, not the height above.
Correct. The disc is about 0.8 mm above the foveola.
The disc is slightly higher than the foveola, not level.
5 mm overstates the height difference.

q: The fetal fissure normally closes at which week?
w: The fetal fissure closes at week 7, the 14 mm stage. Failure leaves an inferior coloboma at 6 o'clock, since the fissure runs along the underside of the optic cup.
k: Fetal fissure closes week 7 (14 mm stage).
decode: The fetal (choroidal) fissure normally closes about WEEK 7. Failure gives an inferonasal coloboma. Not week 3, 12, or 36.
ow: Week 36 is when the hyaloid artery regresses, not fissure closure.
Week 12 is too late for fissure closure.
Week 3 is too early; the optic cup is just forming.
Correct. The fetal fissure closes about week 7.

q: The hyaloid artery has fully regressed by:
w: The hyaloid artery regresses by about week 36. Failure leaves PHPV with leukocoria; benign remnants include Cloquet's canal and a Mittendorf dot on the posterior lens capsule.
k: Hyaloid artery gone by week 36/birth.
decode: The hyaloid artery fully regresses by about WEEK 36 / birth. A remnant after birth is abnormal. Not week 7, 20, or age 2.
ow: Week 7 is far too early; the artery is still active.
By age 2 it is long gone; regression is by birth.
Correct. The hyaloid artery regresses by about week 36 / birth.
Week 20 is too early for full regression.

q: A Mittendorf dot on the posterior lens capsule is:
w: A Mittendorf dot is a harmless remnant of the hyaloid artery's attachment to the posterior lens. It needs no treatment and must not be mistaken for pathology.
k: Mittendorf dot = benign hyaloid remnant.
decode: A Mittendorf dot (small opacity on the posterior lens capsule) is a BENIGN remnant of the hyaloid artery. Not retinoblastoma, cataract, or PHPV.
ow: It is benign, not a retinoblastoma sign.
It is a hyaloid remnant, not a progressive cataract.
PHPV is a larger retrolental mass; a Mittendorf dot is benign.
Correct. A Mittendorf dot is a benign normal variant.

q: The extraocular muscles derive from:
w: The EOMs are mesodermal. The lens and lacrimal gland come from surface ectoderm, the retina from neuroectoderm, and the corneal stroma and endothelium from neural crest.
k: EOMs = mesoderm.
decode: The extraocular muscles derive from MESODERM. Not neuroectoderm, endoderm, or surface ectoderm.
ow: Neuroectoderm forms the retina, not muscles.
Endoderm forms gut lining, not eye muscles.
Surface ectoderm forms the lens, not muscles.
Correct. The extraocular muscles are mesoderm.

q: The lacrimal gland derives from:
w: The lacrimal gland is surface ectoderm, the same origin as the lens and the corneal epithelium.
k: Lacrimal gland = surface ectoderm.
decode: The lacrimal gland derives from SURFACE ECTODERM (like the lens and corneal epithelium). Not neural crest, mesoderm, or neuroectoderm.
ow: Correct. The lacrimal gland is surface ectoderm.
Neural crest forms sclera and corneal stroma.
Mesoderm forms muscles and vessels.
Neuroectoderm forms the retina.

q: Aniridia results from a mutation in which gene?
w: PAX6 is the master control gene of eye development, and its mutation causes aniridia. FBN1 causes Marfan's, so a superotemporal lens dislocation, not an iris defect.
k: Aniridia = PAX6; Marfan = FBN1.
decode: Aniridia is a PAX6 mutation (master eye-development gene). FBN1 is Marfan, COL4A1 is a vascular collagen disorder, RPE65 is a retinal dystrophy gene.
ow: FBN1 causes Marfan, not aniridia.
COL4A1 causes a vascular/collagen disorder.
Correct. Aniridia is a PAX6 mutation.
RPE65 causes Leber congenital amaurosis, not aniridia.

q: The primary vitreous is distinguished from the secondary by being:
w: The primary vitreous is vascular, built around the hyaloid artery, and regresses to leave Cloquet's canal. The secondary vitreous is avascular and becomes the adult gel.
k: Primary vitreous vascular; secondary avascular.
decode: The PRIMARY vitreous is VASCULAR, carrying the hyaloid artery; the secondary is avascular and becomes the adult gel. Vascular = primary.
ow: The primary vitreous is transient, not permanent.
Correct. The primary vitreous is vascular, carrying the hyaloid artery.
The vitreous is neuroectodermal/mesenchymal, not surface ectoderm.
Avascular describes the SECONDARY vitreous.

q: Which term describes convolutions (folds) of the cerebral cortex?
w: Gyri: Greek gyros — circle. Convolutions (folds) of the cerebral cortex
k: Gyri = Convolutions (folds) of the cerebral cortex
decode: The folds (convolutions) of the cortex are the GYRI; the grooves between them are sulci. Gyri = ridges.
ow: Correct. Gyri are the cortical folds (ridges).
Sulci are the grooves between gyri.
The Haversian system is in bone, not brain.
Fissures are the deepest grooves, not the folds.

q: Which term describes deep grooves dividing major brain regions?
w: Fissures: Latin fissura — cleft. Deep grooves dividing major brain regions
k: Fissures = Deep grooves dividing major brain regions
decode: The DEEP grooves dividing major brain regions are FISSURES (deeper than sulci). Fissures = major divisions.
ow: Sulci are shallower grooves, not the major divisions.
The Haversian system is in bone, not brain.
Gyri are the ridges, not grooves.
Correct. Fissures are the deep grooves dividing brain regions.

q: Which term describes the structural unit of compact bone; contains Haversian canals, lamellae, and osteocytes?
w: Haversian system: Named after Clopton Havers. The structural unit of compact bone; contains Haversian canals, lamellae, and osteocytes
k: Haversian system = The structural unit of compact bone; contains Haversian canals, lamellae, and osteocytes
decode: The structural unit of compact bone (Haversian canal, lamellae, osteocytes) is the HAVERSIAN SYSTEM (osteon). The others are brain terms.
ow: Gyri are cortical folds, not bone units.
Correct. The Haversian system (osteon) is the compact-bone unit.
Sulci are brain grooves, not bone units.
Fissures are brain grooves, not bone units.

q: Which term describes three protective membranes covering the brain and spinal cord (dura, arachnoid, pia)?
w: Meninges: Greek meninx — membrane. Three protective membranes covering the brain and spinal cord (dura, arachnoid, pia)
k: Meninges = Three protective membranes covering the brain and spinal cord (dura, arachnoid, pia)
decode: The three protective membranes over the CNS (dura, arachnoid, pia) are the MENINGES. Not gyri, sulci, or fissures.
ow: Gyri are cortical folds, not membranes.
Correct. The meninges are the three protective membranes.
Fissures are brain grooves, not membranes.
Sulci are brain grooves, not membranes.

q: Which term describes membrane-filled gaps between infant skull bones; close as ossification completes?
w: Fontanels: French — soft spot. Membrane-filled gaps between infant skull bones; close as ossification completes
k: Fontanels = Membrane-filled gaps between infant skull bones; close as ossification completes
decode: The membrane-filled gaps between infant skull bones that close with ossification are the FONTANELS ('soft spots'). Not gyri, sulci, or fissures.
ow: Correct. Fontanels are the infant skull soft spots.
Gyri are cortical folds, not skull gaps.
Sulci are brain grooves, not skull gaps.
Fissures are brain grooves, not skull gaps.

q: Which term describes largest foramen in the skull; connects medulla oblongata to spinal cord?
w: Foramen magnum: Latin — large hole. Largest foramen in the skull; connects medulla oblongata to spinal cord
k: Foramen magnum = Largest foramen in the skull; connects medulla oblongata to spinal cord
decode: The largest skull foramen, connecting the medulla to the spinal cord, is the FORAMEN MAGNUM. Not a fissure, sulcus, or gyrus.
ow: Fissures are brain grooves, not a skull foramen.
Sulci are brain grooves, not a foramen.
Gyri are cortical folds, not a foramen.
Correct. The foramen magnum is the largest skull foramen.

q: The optic canal dimensions is:
w: Optic canal dimensions: 4–10 mm long. Completely surrounded by bone inside the lesser wing of sphenoid — protected unless sphenoidal sinusitis erodes through
k: Optic canal dimensions = 4–10 mm long
decode: The optic canal is about 4-10 mm long. The 5.5, 6.9, 7.7 values are rectus insertion distances (spiral of Tillaux), not the canal.
ow: 7.7 mm is the superior rectus insertion distance, not the canal.
6.9 mm is the inferior rectus insertion distance.
5.5 mm is the medial rectus insertion distance.
Correct. The optic canal is about 4-10 mm long.

q: The limbus distance — MR is:
w: Limbus distance — MR: 5.5 mm (nearest). Closest insertion = best mechanical leverage = strongest recti muscle. This is why convergence (both MRs pulling simultaneously) is the most powerful EOM movement
k: Limbus distance — MR = 5.5 mm (nearest)
decode: The medial rectus inserts about 5.5 mm from the limbus (closest of the recti, spiral of Tillaux). The other values are the canal length or other recti.
ow: 6.9 mm is the inferior rectus insertion.
7.7 mm is the superior rectus insertion.
4-10 mm is the optic canal length, not a rectus insertion.
Correct. The medial rectus inserts about 5.5 mm from the limbus.

q: The limbus distance — SR is:
w: Limbus distance — SR: 7.7 mm (farthest). Being farthest means SR pulls at a 23° angle to the visual axis — it cannot produce pure elevation alone. The angle forces secondary intorsion and tertiary adduction as unavoidable byproducts
k: Limbus distance — SR = 7.7 mm (farthest)
decode: The superior rectus inserts about 7.7 mm from the limbus, the farthest of the recti (spiral of Tillaux). The 5.5/6.9 values are other recti.
ow: 5.5 mm is the medial rectus insertion.
6.9 mm is the inferior rectus insertion.
Correct. The superior rectus inserts about 7.7 mm from the limbus.
4-10 mm is the optic canal length, not a rectus insertion.

q: The LR insertion is:
w: LR insertion: 6.9 mm. LR is the only muscle abducting the eye. In CN6 palsy, LR fails and MR acts unopposed — the eye is pulled permanently nasally, producing esotropia. The amount of esotropia tells you how complete the palsy is
k: LR insertion = 6.9 mm
decode: The lateral rectus inserts about 6.9 mm from the limbus (spiral of Tillaux). The 5.5/7.7 values are other recti.
ow: 5.5 mm is the medial rectus insertion.
7.7 mm is the superior rectus insertion.
Correct. The lateral rectus inserts about 6.9 mm from the limbus.
4-10 mm is the optic canal length, not a rectus insertion.

q: The palpebral fissure height is:
w: Palpebral fissure: 8–11 mm height, 27–30 mm width. The normal measurement. Widening (Dalrymple's sign) suggests LPS overaction or Müller's muscle excess, as in thyroid eye disease. Narrowing suggests ptosis or Horner's
k: Palpebral fissure = 8–11 mm height, 27–30 mm width
decode: The palpebral fissure height (open lids) is about 8-11 mm. The single-value distances are rectus insertions or the canal.
ow: 4-10 mm is the optic canal length, not the fissure.
Correct. The palpebral fissure is about 8-11 mm high.
5.5 mm is a rectus insertion distance.
7.7 mm is a rectus insertion distance.

q: The SO total length is:
w: SO total length: 60 mm (longest EOM total). Long because it travels from the orbital apex all the way to the trochlea and then bends back to insert posteriorly — the longest path of any EOM
k: SO total length = 60 mm (longest EOM total)
decode: The superior oblique's total length is about 60 mm (the longest EOM, with its long tendon). The small values are insertion distances.
ow: 5.5 mm is a rectus insertion, not the SO length.
Correct. The superior oblique is about 60 mm total (longest EOM).
4-10 mm is the optic canal length.
7.7 mm is a rectus insertion distance.

q: The IO total length is:
w: IO total length: 37 mm (shortest EOM). Short because it originates near the front of the orbital floor — it has almost no belly, hence no tendon or a minimal 1–2 mm one
k: IO total length = 37 mm (shortest EOM)
decode: The inferior oblique's total length is about 37 mm (the shortest EOM). The small values are insertion distances.
ow: 4-10 mm is the optic canal length.
Correct. The inferior oblique is about 37 mm (shortest EOM).
7.7 mm is a rectus insertion distance.
5.5 mm is a rectus insertion distance.

q: Which term describes the fibrocartilaginous loop on the orbital roof that redirects the SO tendon — acts as a mechanical pulley?
w: Trochlea: Greek trokhilia — pulley. The fibrocartilaginous loop on the orbital roof that redirects the SO tendon — acts as a mechanical pulley
k: Trochlea = The fibrocartilaginous loop on the orbital roof that redirects the SO tendon — acts as a mechanical
decode: The fibrocartilaginous PULLEY on the orbital roof that redirects the superior oblique tendon is the TROCHLEA. The other options are muscle groups or actions.
ow: Adduction is a movement, not the pulley.
Correct. The trochlea is the superior oblique's pulley.
'Oblique' names the muscle, not its pulley.
'Recti' are the straight muscles, not the pulley.

q: Which term describes the four straight muscles that run along the orbital walls?
w: Recti: Latin rectus — straight. The four straight muscles that run along the orbital walls
k: Recti = The four straight muscles that run along the orbital walls
decode: The four STRAIGHT muscles along the orbital walls are the RECTI. The obliques are angled; the trochlea is a pulley.
ow: Correct. The recti are the four straight muscles.
The obliques are angled, not straight.
The trochlea is a pulley, not a muscle group.
Adduction is a movement, not a muscle group.

q: Which term describes the two muscles whose paths are angled relative to the visual axis?
w: Oblique: Latin obliquus — slanting. The two muscles whose paths are angled relative to the visual axis
k: Oblique = The two muscles whose paths are angled relative to the visual axis
decode: The two muscles ANGLED relative to the visual axis are the OBLIQUES. The recti are straight; trochlea is a pulley.
ow: Correct. The obliques are angled to the visual axis.
The trochlea is a pulley, not a muscle group.
The recti run straight, not angled.
Adduction is a movement, not a muscle group.

q: Which term describes moving the eye nasally (toward the midline)?
w: Adduction: Latin ad — toward + ducere — to lead. Moving the eye nasally (toward the midline)
k: Adduction = Moving the eye nasally (toward the midline)
decode: Moving the eye NASALLY (toward the midline) is ADDUCTION. Abduction is temporal; the others are structures.
ow: Correct. Adduction moves the eye nasally.
The trochlea is a pulley, not a movement.
'Recti' are muscles, not a movement.
'Oblique' names muscles, not this movement.

q: Which term describes moving the eye temporally (away from midline)?
w: Abduction: Latin ab — away + ducere — to lead. Moving the eye temporally (away from midline)
k: Abduction = Moving the eye temporally (away from midline)
decode: Moving the eye TEMPORALLY (away from midline) is ABDUCTION. Adduction is nasal; the others are structures.
ow: The trochlea is a pulley, not a movement.
'Recti' are muscles, not a movement.
'Oblique' names muscles, not a movement.
Correct. Abduction moves the eye temporally.

q: Which term describes the thinnest orbital wall (medial, ethmoid bone) — the wall that fractures first?
w: Lamina papyracea: Latin — paper-thin plate. The thinnest orbital wall (medial, ethmoid bone) — the wall that fractures first
k: Lamina papyracea = The thinnest orbital wall (medial, ethmoid bone) — the wall that fractures first
decode: The thinnest orbital wall (medial, ethmoid) is the LAMINA PAPYRACEA ('paper layer'), the wall that fractures and transmits infection first. The others are muscle terms.
ow: Correct. The lamina papyracea is the thin medial wall.
'Oblique' names a muscle, not a wall.
The trochlea is a pulley, not a wall.
'Recti' are muscles, not a wall.

q: The upper tarsus height is:
w: Upper tarsus height: 11 mm. LPS inserts here — LPS paralysis = complete ptosis; Müller's paralysis = 1–2mm ptosis
k: Upper tarsus height = 11 mm
decode: The UPPER tarsus is about 11 mm tall (larger than the lower). The lower tarsus is about 5 mm.
ow: 3 mm is too short for the upper tarsus.
5 mm is the LOWER tarsus height.
Correct. The upper tarsus is about 11 mm tall.
20 mm is too tall for a tarsus.

q: The lower tarsus height is:
w: Lower tarsus height: 5 mm. Lower lid has less tarsal support — explains lower lid laxity with age
k: Lower tarsus height = 5 mm

q: The lacrimal punctum size is:

q: The canaliculus horizontal length is:

q: The lacrimal sac dimensions is:

5 mm is the lower tarsus, not the duct.

q: Which term describes sebaceous glands embedded in the tarsus; produce the oily lipid layer of the tear film?
w: Meibomian glands: Named after Heinrich Meibom (1638–1700). Sebaceous glands embedded in the tarsus; produce the oily lipid layer of the tear film

The punctum is a drainage opening, not a gland.
The fornix is a conjunctival pocket, not a gland.

q: Which term describes anything related to the eyelid (palpebral conjunctiva, palpebral fissure, pars palpebralis)?
w: Palpebral: Latin palpebra — eyelid. Anything related to the eyelid (palpebral conjunctiva, palpebral fissure, pars palpebralis)
k: Palpebral = Anything related to the eyelid (palpebral conjunctiva, palpebral fissure, pars palpebralis)

Correct. 'Palpebral' pertains to the eyelid.
Meibomian glands are lid glands, but not this general term.
The fornix is a conjunctival pocket, not the eyelid term.

q: Which term describes the fold of conjunctiva at the deepest part where the eyelid conjunctiva meets the bulbar conjunctiva; the "pocket" of conjunctival space?
w: Fornix: Latin — arch, vault. The fold of conjunctiva at the deepest part where the eyelid conjunctiva meets the bulbar conjunctiva; the "pocket" of conjunctival space
k: Fornix = The fold of conjunctiva at the deepest part where the eyelid conjunctiva meets the bulbar conjunctiva
decode: The conjunctival FOLD where lid meets bulbar conjunctiva, the deep 'pocket', is the FORNIX. The others are glands or openings.

'Palpebral' is a general eyelid term, not the pocket.
The punctum is a drainage opening, not the pocket.
Correct. The fornix is the conjunctival pocket.

q: Which term describes the tiny opening at the medial end of each eyelid through which tears enter the drainage system?
w: Punctum: Latin — point. The tiny opening at the medial end of each eyelid through which tears enter the drainage system
k: Punctum = The tiny opening at the medial end of each eyelid through which tears enter the drainage system
decode: The tiny medial-lid opening where tears ENTER drainage is the PUNCTUM. The others are glands, pockets, or general terms.
ow: Correct. The punctum is the tear-drainage opening.
Meibomian glands make oil, they are not the opening.
The fornix is the conjunctival pocket, not the opening.
'Palpebral' is a general eyelid term.

q: Which term describes the narrow tube connecting the punctum to the lacrimal sac?
w: Canaliculus: Latin — small canal. The narrow tube connecting the punctum to the lacrimal sac
k: Canaliculus = The narrow tube connecting the punctum to the lacrimal sac
decode: The narrow tube from punctum to lacrimal sac is the CANALICULUS. The others are glands, pockets, or general terms.
ow: Correct. The canaliculus connects punctum to sac.
Meibomian glands make oil, not a drainage tube.
'Palpebral' is a general eyelid term.
The fornix is the conjunctival pocket.

q: Which term describes the duct that carries tears from the lacrimal sac into the nasal cavity?
w: Nasolacrimal: Naso (nose) + lacrimal (tear). The duct that carries tears from the lacrimal sac into the nasal cavity

ow: 'Palpebral' is a general eyelid term, not the duct.
Meibomian glands make oil, not the duct.
The fornix is the conjunctival pocket.
Correct. The nasolacrimal duct drains tears into the nose.

q: Which term describes unicellular glands in the conjunctival epithelium that secrete mucin?
w: Goblet cell: Named for their goblet/cup shape. Unicellular glands in the conjunctival epithelium that secrete mucin
k: Goblet cell = Unicellular glands in the conjunctival epithelium that secrete mucin
decode: The unicellular conjunctival glands secreting MUCIN are the GOBLET cells. The others are lid glands, pockets, or general terms.

Meibomian glands make lipid, not mucin.
'Palpebral' is a general eyelid term.

q: Which term describes time in seconds from last blink to first dry spot on cornea — measures tear film stability?
w: TBUT: Tear Break-Up Time. Time in seconds from last blink to first dry spot on cornea — measures tear film stability
k: TBUT = Time in seconds from last blink to first dry spot on cornea — measures tear film stability
decode: The seconds from the last blink to the first dry spot (tear-film stability) is the TBUT (tear breakup time). The others are anatomical terms.
ow: 'Palpebral' is a general eyelid term, not a test.
The fornix is a conjunctival pocket, not a test.

Meibomian glands make oil; they are not the test.

q: Which term describes swelling/edema of the conjunctiva, most prominent at the loose fornix?
w: Chemosis: Greek kheme — clam shell (gaping shell). Swelling/edema of the conjunctiva, most prominent at the loose fornix
k: Chemosis = Swelling/edema of the conjunctiva, most prominent at the loose fornix
decode: Swelling/edema of the conjunctiva, ballooning at the loose fornix, is CHEMOSIS. The others are anatomical terms, not the edema.
ow: The fornix is where chemosis pools, but the swelling itself is chemosis.

'Palpebral' is a general eyelid term, not edema.
Meibomian glands make oil; they are not conjunctival edema.

q: The corneal central thickness is:
w: Corneal central thickness: 0.52–0.56 mm. Measured by pachymeter — thin cornea = risk in refractive surgery; thick = suspect IOP readings

q: The corneal peripheral thickness is:
w: Corneal peripheral thickness: 0.7–1.0 mm. Cornea thickens toward the periphery

0.52-0.56 mm is the CENTRAL thickness.
Correct. Peripheral corneal thickness is about 0.7-1.0 mm.
11-12 mm is the corneal diameter.

q: The corneal radius of curvature is:
w: Corneal radius of curvature: 7–8.5 mm (avg 7.8 mm). Steeper cornea = more power. Keratoconus = cone shape = irregular steep curvature

Correct. The corneal radius of curvature is about 7-8.5 mm.
0.7-1.0 mm is peripheral thickness, not radius.
11-12 mm is the corneal diameter.

q: The corneal horizontal diameter is:
w: Corneal horizontal diameter: 11–12 mm. Wider than vertical (10–11mm) — cornea is a horizontal oval, not a circle
k: Corneal horizontal diameter = 11–12 mm
decode: The horizontal corneal diameter is about 11-12 mm. The small values are thicknesses; 7-8.5 is radius.

0.52-0.56 mm is central thickness.
7-8.5 mm is the radius of curvature.
0.7-1.0 mm is peripheral thickness.

q: The scleral thickness at CN2 is:
w: Scleral thickness at CN2: 1.0 mm (thickest). Most protected region
k: Scleral thickness at CN2 = 1.0 mm (thickest)
decode: The sclera is thickest (about 1.0 mm) at the optic nerve (CN2) entrance. Thinnest is under the recti.

Correct. Scleral thickness at the optic nerve is about 1.0 mm.
0.52-0.56 mm is corneal, not scleral, thickness.

q: The scleral thickness at recti is:
w: Scleral thickness at recti: 0.3 mm (thinnest). Site of staphyloma, risk area for perforation in surgery
k: Scleral thickness at recti = 0.3 mm (thinnest)

0.52-0.56 mm is corneal thickness.
Correct. Scleral thickness under the recti is about 0.3 mm.
7-8.5 mm is the corneal radius, not scleral thickness.

q: The scleral radius of curvature is:
w: Scleral radius of curvature: 12 mm. Flatter than cornea; not refractive
k: Scleral radius of curvature = 12 mm
decode: The scleral radius of curvature is about 12 mm (larger, flatter than the ~7.8 mm cornea). The thin values are thicknesses.

0.7-1.0 mm is a thickness, not a radius.
7-8.5 mm is the CORNEAL radius.
0.52-0.56 mm is corneal thickness.

q: Which term describes the tough white outer coat that forms 5/6 of the eyeball wall?

q: Which term describes the 1–2 mm transition zone where cornea meets sclera — not just anatomical, but clinically critical (contains drainage angle)?
w: Limbus: Latin — border, threshold. The 1–2 mm transition zone where cornea meets sclera — not just anatomical, but clinically critical (contains drainage angle)

q: Which term describes the thick middle layer of the cornea (90% of its thickness); the "mattress" of collagen?

q: Which term describes the basement membrane of the endothelium — elastic, resistant to perforation?
w: Descemet's membrane: Named after Jean Descemet (18th c.). The basement membrane of the endothelium — elastic, resistant to perforation

The scleral spur is an angle landmark, not a corneal layer.

q: Which term describes a balloon-like protrusion of Descemet's membrane through a perforated corneal stroma — the stroma gives way but Descemet holds?

q: Which term describes the innermost single-cell layer of the cornea; critical for deturgescence via Na-K pump?
w: Endothelium: Greek endon — within + thele — nipple. The innermost single-cell layer of the cornea; critical for deturgescence via Na-K pump

ow: The limbus is the cornea-sclera junction, not a cell layer.
The sclera is the outer coat.
Correct. The endothelium is the innermost single-cell layer with the pump.
The stroma is the thick middle layer, not the pump layer.

q: Which term describes the active dehydration of the corneal stroma maintained by the endothelial pump?
w: Deturgescence: Latin de — away + turgescere — to swell. The active dehydration of the corneal stroma maintained by the endothelial pump
k: Deturgescence = The active dehydration of the corneal stroma maintained by the endothelial pump
decode: Active dehydration of the corneal stroma by the endothelial pump is DETURGESCENCE (staying clear by staying dry). The others are structures.
ow: The sclera is the outer coat, not this process.
The stroma is the layer kept dry, not the process itself.
The limbus is the junction, not this process.
Correct. Deturgescence is the pump-driven stromal dehydration.

q: Which term describes the instrument that measures corneal thickness?
w: Pachymeter: Greek pakhys — thick + metron — measure. The instrument that measures corneal thickness
k: Pachymeter = The instrument that measures corneal thickness
decode: The instrument that measures corneal thickness is the PACHYMETER ('pachy' = thick). The others are anatomical terms.

The sclera is the outer coat, not an instrument.
Correct. A pachymeter measures corneal thickness.
The limbus is the cornea-sclera junction, not an instrument.

q: Which term describes the flat, stellate cells within the corneal stroma that produce and maintain the collagen matrix?
w: Keratocyte: Greek keras — horn + kytos — cell. The flat, stellate cells within the corneal stroma that produce and maintain the collagen matrix
k: Keratocyte = The flat, stellate cells within the corneal stroma that produce and maintain the collagen matrix
decode: The flat, stellate stromal cells that make and maintain corneal collagen are the KERATOCYTES. The others are structures.
ow: The limbus is the junction, not a cell.
The sclera is the outer coat, not a cell.
The stroma is the layer these cells live in, not the cell name.
Correct. Keratocytes maintain the stromal collagen.

q: Which term describes channels through the sclera through which nerves and vessels pass?
w: Emissarium: Latin — outlet. Channels through the sclera through which nerves and vessels pass
k: Emissarium = Channels through the sclera through which nerves and vessels pass
decode: The scleral channels for nerves and vessels are the EMISSARIA (emissarium). The others are structures.

The limbus is the cornea-sclera junction, not a channel.
Correct. Emissaria are the scleral channels for nerves and vessels.

0.25 mm is a choroid thickness.

q: The choroid posterior thickness is:

3-4 mm is the pupil size, not choroid thickness.

w: Choroid anterior thickness: 0.10 mm (thinnest). Near ora serrata
k: Choroid anterior thickness = 0.10 mm (thinnest)
decode: The choroid thins to about 0.10 mm ANTERIORLY (near the ora). Posteriorly it is ~0.25 mm.
ow: Correct. The anterior choroid is about 0.10 mm thick.
0.25 mm is the POSTERIOR choroid thickness.
6 mm is the ciliary body width.
3-4 mm is the pupil size.

q: Which term describes named for the variety of colors it can display; the visible colored ring of the eye?
w: Iris: Greek — rainbow. Named for the variety of colors it can display; the visible colored ring of the eye

Mydriasis is pupil dilation, not the colored ring.
The collarette is a ridge on the iris, not the whole iris.
Correct. The iris is the colored ring of the eye.

q: Which term describes the circular ridge on the iris that separates the pupillary zone from the ciliary zone?
w: Collarette: French — small collar. The circular ridge on the iris that separates the pupillary zone from the ciliary zone
k: Collarette = The circular ridge on the iris that separates the pupillary zone from the ciliary zone
decode: The circular ridge dividing the iris pupillary zone from the ciliary zone is the COLLARETTE. The others are the whole iris or pupil sizes.
ow: Mydriasis is pupil dilation, not the ridge.
The iris is the whole structure, not this ridge.
Correct. The collarette separates the pupillary and ciliary zones.
Miosis is pupil constriction, not the ridge.

q: Which term describes named for the fringe-like ciliary processes; the production site of aqueous and the motor of accommodation?
w: Ciliary body: Latin cilia — eyelashes. Named for the fringe-like ciliary processes; the production site of aqueous and the motor of accommodation

Correct. The ciliary body makes aqueous and drives accommodation.
Miosis is pupil constriction, not a structure.
The collarette is an iris ridge, not the ciliary body.

q: Which term describes the flat, non-vascular posterior portion of the ciliary body — preferred surgical entry site?
w: Pars plana: Latin — flat part. The flat, non-vascular posterior portion of the ciliary body — preferred surgical entry site
k: Pars plana = The flat, non-vascular posterior portion of the ciliary body — preferred surgical entry site
decode: The flat, non-vascular POSTERIOR ciliary body (safe surgical entry) is the PARS PLANA. The pars plicata is the folded anterior part; the others are iris terms.

The collarette is an iris ridge, not the ciliary body.
Miosis is pupil constriction, not a structure.
The iris is the colored ring, not the ciliary body.

q: Which term describes the folded, vascular anterior portion with ciliary processes — produces aqueous?
w: Pars plicata: Latin — folded part. The folded, vascular anterior portion with ciliary processes — produces aqueous
k: Pars plicata = The folded, vascular anterior portion with ciliary processes — produces aqueous

The collarette is an iris ridge, not the ciliary body.
Miosis is pupil constriction, not a structure.

q: Which term describes the innermost vascular layer of the choroid — wide-bore capillaries that supply the outer retina?
w: Choriocapillaris: Greek khorion — membrane + capillary. The innermost vascular layer of the choroid — wide-bore capillaries that supply the outer retina
k: Choriocapillaris = The innermost vascular layer of the choroid — wide-bore capillaries that supply the outer r

ow: Correct. The choriocapillaris supplies the outer retina.
The iris is the colored ring, not a choroidal layer.
The collarette is an iris ridge, not a choroidal layer.
Miosis is pupil constriction, not a layer.

q: Which term describes the thin innermost layer of the choroid separating it from the RPE?
w: Bruch's membrane: Named after Karl Wilhelm Ludwig Bruch. The thin innermost layer of the choroid separating it from the RPE
k: Bruch's membrane = The thin innermost layer of the choroid separating it from the RPE
